Grading is pretty easy.
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Solid class. Professor could be more organized, but helpful perspectives and great information with the speaker series. Herb is awesome!!!
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Overall it's a very practical class - teaches you how to look at accounting without having to be an accountant. Helpful if you plan on being in the c-suite later in your career. Guest speakers are also amazing. The only downside is the professor is incredibly disorganized.
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments:
there are a lot of assignments but they do not take a lot of time. Make sure you pay attention to the syllabus to not miss anything
 I think this class is useful for anyone who has aspirations to the C suite because if you do you will be working with a CFO most likely. I loved loved this class
 Herb and the guest speakers he brings in are incredible~

comments: The class is relax and you can choose your group

topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: The class brings in CFOs to talk about their business (Skims, Revolve, Costco, East West Bank) which is cool. The early mornings were tough.
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Pretty high level when it comes to finance, not a lot of hard valuation/analysis skills developed. topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Cool class. The professor brings in great speakers. The coursework was practical and worthwhile.
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: I think if you took his class seriously and practiced looking through 10-Ks and stuff it may be helpful. However, I think that his teaching style isn't the most engaging, but his guest speakers are pretty good.=
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: The class is relax and you can choose your group
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: He brings in very cool guest speakers. However, I would have appreciated the class more if he covered few basics before diving into strategies
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Solid workload but very manageable. Professor Perlmutter brings in some amazing guest speakers and has a great network to pull from. My biggest qualm is that he sticks to his script to much, he is his best when you get him chatting about his experience, the class can be dry if you're not asking questions.
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Highly recommend Prof. Herb’s class! The course includes around eight cases, each structured as a sequence of introduction → alternative strategy discussion → simulated board meeting → guest speaker. It offers a deep dive into various industries through a financial analysis lens. The workload is relatively heavy, but absolutely worth it!
topic_title: ACCT 559 - Strategy and Operations Through CFO Lens

comments: Not knowledgeble. We miss professor Trazevant

Under the previous professor, Trezevant, this was a great class. Sadly, Trezevant passed away in February 2015, and this substitute has not done the class justice. Trezevant was known for his teaching method, and this professor does not have the same ability to teach, and unfortunately has rendered this class and its syllabus useless.
You don't learn anything past core accounting in this class. Moreover, the professor is quite dry, though he knows A LOT about tax law.
Great content and professor (T.J. Wong)! Class is case based and really informative. Real world examples provide a great tool for discussion and learning.

Poor teacher, despite practitioner experience.
 
Professor reads from slides prepared by textbook company. While he understands real-world accounting and auditing, he does not show mastering of the syllabus or the subject matter for any given class session. He is able to explain answers to HW questions, but not able to actually demonstrate how to do the HW.
 
 Shows little interest in wrestling through students' intuitions to establish real understanding. Asks students, "are we all getting this" rather than using cold-calling and case method to see how students are actually understanding the material.
 
USC clearly brought in a brilliant practitioner, then failed to instill functional pedagogy.

Content is amazing. Really delves deep into the namesake of the course "Financial Statements Analysis". K.R. is funny and engaging and a wealth of knowledge. I will caveat that the lectures can be very dense. This man takes up the entire time block, every single second, hammering into you all that is financial accounting analysis.

The class is based on the discussion of cases from 8 different countries, highlighting the differences in terms of market structure, culture, and company ownership. This differences impact the way companies do business, treat shareholders and compete in the market. 
The class discusses topics that I haven't seen in other Marshall classes, like family business, board of directors structures, company ownership structure and shareholders incentives. Although it is a ACCT class, it is not a traditional accounting class, the discussions are focused on strategy and incentives, and some impacts on accounting and standards, but you won't do any accounting job here.
topic_title: ACCT 574 - Accounting and Corporate Governance in Global Business

comments: This class is fascinating. A deep look at corporate governance and power structures and how they play out in different societal and cultural environments. Feels much more like a Liberal Arts meets Business course than an accounting course.

comments: [useful field] not particularly but the content is interesting and i think the information is important
topic_title: ACCT 574 - Accounting and Corporate Governance in Global Business

comments: TJ is a bit disorganized (we tend to not cover the material that he has set aside for that given lecture), but his tests are open-book, open-note and extremely fair. The large majority of the class are MSAcct students and there are two group cases, as an FYI. He also takes attendance for every class.
topic_title: ACCT 574 - Accounting and Corporate Governance in Global Business

comments: The professor is a bit disorganized. I definitely learned a lot, but more structure would have helped.

Very good class and professor. Covers a lot of material within a short period of time.. If you are a finance guy, this class would be a breeze. Otherwise, prepare to put in a solid 5-6 hours of effort (weekly) to learn the concepts well. He is very lenient when it comes to grading.
Solid class where you learn to pick a part company's financials. It can be a little accounting heavy but is definitely worth it. He uses a lot of his experience which is helpful.

Class can be like watching paint dry BUT it is an extremely valuable course, and taught accounting from a high-level perspective like I wish we had learned in CORE. Heitzman cares that we learn the stuff and will teach it at any level in office hours. Lots of work, lots of value.
A deeper look at accounting learned in Core. A lot of group projects and quizzes (instead of midterm) which can be time consuming.

The material is great. However the professor lacks structure. A major part of the class are accounting students and the professor doesn't account for the fact that the MBA's are not at a high 'accounting' level. Monotonous tone of lectures makes it hard to keep interested.

It's a good class to take if you are not clear about accounting. I wish he was the core accounting prof. He doesn't like to be questioned, but overall humorous young professor. It's a combo of valuations, accounting tricks to look at on public company filings. I've learned a lot.

The content of the class is fair. The professor covered most of important concepts and issues in accounting. Yet personally I think some of the contents were way to detailed. Also the decks were not highly organized -- it is somehow hard to read and follow for me. Only 3 this class to someone who is going to do related careers like financial analyst or accountant.
Professors slides in class are terrible. Makes basic ideas complex and confusing.
This is what the core Accounting should be. Just enough accounting to understand how to work with financial statements, forecasting, and valuing companies. This is what MBAs do, not T balances.

It was good exposure to financial statements, though the class could have taken a much deeper dive on the issues. I feel like at the end of the class I had stronger understanding of the mechanics of accounting, but not necessarily being able to interpret how healthy a company was based on their financial statements.
Excellent class for a person like myself that wants to get better at finance.
The concepts covered are very important but the professor is not very effective in explaining them. I would take the class with a different professor.

"Professor is the worst. Why?
1. His teaching style is very slow, his voice is slow and his slides the most unhelpful.
2. He doesnt know how to teach to MBA students. 
3. His syllabus is the worst I have seen. No dates of when the quizzes or the assignments are due. 

Having said that, the class is really useful."

"Shane is really bright and knows his stuff inside and out. However this sometimes has the effect of getting really into the weeds and overwhelm students who are new to the material.

He was one of the worst profs I've had at Marshall. The class should be worthwhile but he is really, really bad.

The content is very useful if you want to learn how to understand a company's health just by looking at its account statements. But the professor is not useful in helping you learn that at all. You can learn better from the book, and if possible, the other professor.

Terrible class, terrible professor. He taught directly from the text book slides so you can teach yourself by reading the book & slides. The professor is "older" and his lectures fail to connect with the class. Very monotone. I can't say I learned a lot from this class. If you can take with another professor.

This course was very useful for someone interested in finance or accounting. You spend a lot of time reviewing 10k's and learning the in's-and-out's of how to read them. More importantly, you learn how to read between the lines to see what is really happening in an company's operations, investing, and financing. Workload and grading was average difficulty.

Jim is a former CFO of several companies. His class is run in a business like manner. There is no wasted time or effort. He is incredibly easy to learn difficult content from. You will be blown away with how quickly he provides feedback on homework assignments, exams, and presentations. Jim is one of the rare professors that can talk about a subject and provide personal experience and examples to make the content that much easier to grasp.

The curriculum is beautifully crafted, and the workload is also balanced. 
 On the other hand, the most of the concepts don't need explanation, can be studied remotely.
The professor makes the accounting very easy to understand

Professor Sloan deserves a Golden Apple Award! This professor makes a seemingly complex topic for those not in finance simple. He covers current events, provides his own opinions (he has been cited in major investment publications and does his own investing), and understands how to communicate with students.He really puts effort in to make the course relevant instead of pasting bullet points on slides. I now feel confident reading 10ks and interpreting financial statements so that I as a marketing manager can hold conversations with executives and leadership about the health of the business, company, and competitors. Can't recommend this teacher and class enough.

Richard Sloan was a very well-respected professor at Berkeley, and this is his first semester teaching here at Marshall. I highly recommend taking his class. The course content focuses on how to use accounting principles to tell if a company is undervalued or overvalued in the market. What I like is that he acknowledges that there are many ways to do valuation and then makes a case for the accounting methods he teaches. He also brings in a lot of real world examples (with a heavy focus on Apple this semester) to show how the accounting and business decisions we see in the news impact their economic value. I'm not at all an accounting person, but I found the class fascinating.

I didn't come in with a strong finance or accounting background before pursuing my MBA. This class was a great overview of both subjects in my second year with real world applications for evaluating companies. Also, Professor Sloan is a great teacher who know how to manage and plan a course to ensure learning.
Prof. Sloan is AMAZING. He really does his best to provide students with any and all materials they will need to be successful. He cares a lot and is always open to improving.

Great professor! He brings in relevant current events in the context of finance and combines that with a practical financial statement analysis curriculum

Professor Sloan provides a step-by-step approach for analyzing financial statements. I wish I had taken the course prior to my internship, but I'm excited that I'll have it for my full-time position.

This course was not useful for my current goals, but I wanted to get better at reading financial statements and this course is good for that.  I've heard that the other professor, Leonetti, is really good.  Sloan is decent--definitely an accomplished professor, sometimes funny, but also sometimes extremely slow.  ~10% of each class is spent figuring out the projector or the slides or some other technical difficulties.  That being said, if you're invested in the course material you will get a lot out of it.  5 cases, all done in groups, varying in workload.  Overall a decent class--not awful, not amazing either.
The class is really fast-paced and the book is not great at all. It's too much content for someone who is not going into accounting. I wouldn't suggest this class as a "stretch" course.

Leonetti is one of the best professors I've had at Marshall. He really knows how to engage the class and make the course relevant and interesting, and we get hands on experience analyzing a company of our choice throughout the semester.

This class was definitely out of my comfort zone since I do not come from a quant background. However, it did give me the right amount of information to review the basic accounting/finance principles we learned in 1st year. The professor is great at explaining, and does not cold call. The work load includes group assignments that are manageable. Highly recommend for those who want a refresher course, and want to reinforce the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flows.
You will learn useful skills to analyse F/S and find a more reasonable value of firms, but a bit challenging if you don't have accounting backgrounds.

This class has provided me important skills I was looking for in business school. While I don't think I will ever be a pro at valuation or forecasting I appreciate the high level learnings I will leave this class with. If accounting is indeed the language of business, I will come out of this class at least a conversational speaker.

This was my "challenging" class for the semester - and I'm so glad I took it. I can finally see Accounting and Finance coming together by revisiting some concepts from Core classes. Prof. Sloan's pace is great if you are not an expert! Workload is a little too much but I don't see any other way to make us learn so much in just one semester.

This professor is extremely knowledgable about the area. He is great on missed classes as long as you inform him beforehand, it will not count against you. The HW is extremely easy and the grading is very fair.

Professor is very good with explaining the concepts in the class. He runs at a good pace and is always open to meet outside class if required. He also has a lot of contacts and is of great help when searching for jobs/internships. The assignments are simple and not time consuming. They can also be done in groups.

The lectures are very dry but the professor does a good job teaching the material and the homeworks force you to actually learn how to read a financial statement. By no means an exhilirating class but would recommend for anyone wanting a strong base layer in understanding financial statements.
[useful field] Yes, felt like I learned what I should have learned from the accounting core class. Regular homeworks teach you how to go through financial statements, perform analyses, and create forecasts.

^^ agree with this above - great content and you'll learn, but it isn't exciting by any means
[useful field] To anyone who came to B-school in the hopes of learning something about accounting, this is the class for you.

The lectures can be dense and a bit dry, yet Professor Aaron makes the class as interesting as he can. This class is a great introduction to accounting at a high level and also provides an excellent introduction to how to analyze and forecast financial statements.

This course did not materialize into the class that I had set my expectations on prior to this semester. It is extremely accounting heavy - if you struggled/had to put in a lot of effort in Corporate Finance and courses like Financial Analysis & Valuation, this one is even harder. Plus, there are Masters of Accounting students in this class as well as people targeting Banking; simply put, you need to have intermediate to advanced level of Accounting and Finance knowledge to stay afloat in KR's class. The professor can also be very condescending at times and assumes that you already know a lot of the things he is teaching. Recommend going for Sloan's class in the Fall semester; don't waste your bid points on this one.

Take this course if you expect to be combing through a lot of financial statements (as the course name suggests). The course isn't about creating financial statements, but making assumptions/decisions based on looking at different statements. KR is a nice guy. A little unstructured sometimes. We're simultaneously behind and ahead.

Famous professor but it was hard to follow his style of delivery. I know I'm not the only one zoning out in this class. Great content though. He keeps us updated with the latest current financial and accounting news and practices, asking probing questions and keeps us abreast of things to watch unfold in the real world. Very practical so if you can concentrate and not zone out you will learn a lot that you will actually use out of the classroom.
Interesting class. There is some overlap with the Financial Valuations class, and the same concepts are taught in a slightly different way so it can be a little confusing to reconcile.

A bit fast for my liking but still would recommend the course. You can easily ask questions if you are not able to follow as it gets a bit hard to follow as the professsor changes the focus of discussion very quickly. Need to pay attention in class to be able to get value out of this class
The professor is extremely acomplished in the industry. The class is very hands on and gives you the opportunity to put learnings into practice.

This professor is one of the best professors at USC. He is extremely knowledegable & such a gem. It helps to have a little bit of a finance/accounting background otherwise the material goes pretty quick. If you do the readings/assigments - it's very manageable.
Fantastic professor. Highly recommended class. Very real world applicable content that you would struggle to find outside of Marshall. But a bit challenging though.

Professor K.R. really helps you dive deep into a 10K and sift out the bullshit. Sometimes, even GAAP compliant financial statements tell a deceptive story. Professor K.R. does a great job of teaching the quantitative skills to understanding the nuances of the B/S, I/S, and C/F. Attendance is taken.

Professor K.R. is clearly knowledgeable and the class material is useful. The first half served as a review of Mark Soliman's class and we are now heading into a more analytical framework which is a welcome change. I don't have anything extremely negative to say about the professor, but just do not find him to be the most inspiring lecturer. I do enjoy his sense of humor. The syllabus is a little unclear and disorganized as we progress. I find it difficult to track which readings/homeworks I should be doing to follow along.

Sloan somehow makes financial statements interesting, which is impressive, but he tends to breeze through complicated topics quickly, assuming you have retained 100% of the content from the Accounting core course, which you have not and will come to realize very quickly.
Sloan's great and worth taking it for him if you are remotely interested in better understanding financial statements.

Subject is extremely dry and hard. Moreover a majority of students are not from MBA program and they were from accounting and finance programs. So, might be slightly disadvantageous in the final curve of scores as the others are quite familira with most of the topics

It is still a foundational course following the core accounting one. It gives a deeper layer of analysing statements and learns a lot! The professor is absolutely knowledgeable but the assignment is a lot and hard though.
Professor is great and is willing to repeat or answer any questions. Builds a lot on your accounting basics as you go into more depth. Assignments are hard and can be a lot though

Professor is passionate and has a lot experience but often he just assumes that most of the students knows certain concepts and goes fast. It could have been better if he takes time to explain important concepts and goes step by step
If you want to build off of the basics picked up in 510 and get more in depth on applications of financial data points this course is excellent
Fundamental class but assignments are very handy - you basically learning through doing assignment.

KR is a great professor and presents the material in a very clear way. It doesn't make a whole lot of sense to have a team project and an exam towards the end. I am all for classes that break up deliverables in chunks of equal weights. There are more important things than becoming a sweat shop of deliverables at the tail end of the semester (e.g. recruiting).
Professor is passionate and brings up insightful perspective for financial statement analysis.
Great professor that makes info easy to understand.

topic_title: ACCT 582 - Accounting for Mergers and Acquisitions

comments: The class is important for any future investment banking or investment professional. Half of the class is comprised of the tax consequences of M&A transactions and half is related to the accounting for M&A transactions. The material is advanced and it moves at a fast pace, but it's very valuable learning experience and the coursework is directly applicable to anyone entering IB/VC/PE or working on M&A transactions.
topic_title: ACCT 582 - Accounting for Mergers and Acquisitions

comments: The two parts of this class will be separated going forward, Professor Wang (for the tax part) is very good - clear, concise and instructive.

comments: Class is great for understanding the tax and basic accounting implications of M&A structures. Most students are focusing on careers in IB or finance, however the class is high level enough for non-IB/finance students to gain solid insight into the M&A world.
topic_title: ACCT 582 - Accounting for Mergers and Acquisitions

comments:
This is a split class taught by Shiing-Wu Wang and Patrick Dennis Kinsella . Wang taught the taxation part and Kinsella taught the accounting part.

Despite the dullness of taxation, Wang did an amazing job teaching the subject. He would go breakdown the complex tax concepts into simple and relatable chunks that were easy to understand. Definitely 3 the part with Wang.

Kinsella is a different story. He's a former KPMG partner, but he's really not good at teaching. His classes are really really slow and dry.
topic_title: ACCT 582 - Accounting for Mergers and Acquisitions

comments: This is a challenging class that requires a strong time commitment to stay on top of the material. The first half of the class is strongly focused on tax implications for M&A. If this is the career area you are definitely interested in pursuing it teaches a lot of useful material; but if not I would not recommend.
topic_title: ACCT 582 - Accounting for Mergers and Acquisitions

comments: actually divided into tax planning part and accounting part for each semester. Prof. Wang is really kind and helpful, the exam is open-booked and quite straightforward. Worth taking if you wish to know some IB and tax planning knowledge in M&A.

comments: Not a very good course

Jack and Cynthia are some of the nicest professors you will find at Marshall. Seriously, they are super nice. They sometimes even bring avocados or other gifts for students. Knapp has applicable professional experience having built a company from the ground up and through his current role of investing in new ventures. The class content could have been more applicable, but overall I had a positive experience with the course.
A little bit tightly packed, but a good introduction and exposure. Glad I am taking it. Class is also engaging.

Still very early in the class so it is hard to know. The professor's personality isn't my favorite but he clearly knows what he is talking about and provides many opportunities to learn in useful ways as opposed to just talking at students as so many professors do.

Great class but go into it knowing the golden rule about entrepreneurship...its about getting sh*t done! If you're not interested in hustling to get something to market and putting yourself out there don't bother. Tommy is awesome and makes this very clear. This class is all about energy so don't take it as a schedule filler or you'll just be taking away from your fellow classmates and you also won't learn anything practical so it will be a waste of your money.
Great prof! Learn a lot about starting your own business. He brings in a lot of great speakers. HOWEVER, there is a lot of work involved. He put a full semester of work into a half semester class.
A very lively professor teaching an excellent course. Hands on entrepreneurial projects and real life entrepreneurs coming in to give guest lectures. Definitely 3 this class to everyone.

I want a class like this to focus more on the actual steps that must be done (idea generation, types of funding, stakeholder interviews, etc.) and less on the general story of starting a new business.
Fun class, a little disorganized. The activities we do are cool and the professor is hilarious.

This is a pre-requisite course for other entrepreneurship classes. It was very helpful in setting up a framework for how to think about entrepreneurship and the creation of business. Good projects give you a feel for starting a business but class sessions are often not very useful.

The class is very unstructured which can be a little frustrating sometimes. The teacher is experienced and has a lot of interesting things to say, but a lot of the learning is done in the textbooks which are pretty comprehensive and easy to read. I leave almost every class thinking we didn't really do anything...but I still feel like I'm getting a good idea of what it takes to start a business (albeit mainly from the readings).
This class was really fun and he has unique ways of engaging the class.  Improptu class trips to see new ventures or innovative tech companies were a plus.
Must take as a prerequisite

Good class to introduce the ideas behind starting a company, but focuses mainly on "lifestyle companies," i.e. you're not going to create the next Facebook. I've heard that the other introductory entrepreneurship class is better.
It's a decent class to take if you have a new venture that you are planning on launching soon, but otherwise can be tedious.
Demanding professor and great exposure to successful entrepreneurs, but his description of the VC funding environment wasn't at all what I encountered during my summer internship.

Ivan has a lot of experience and is still working in the space, so has a lot of recent lessons learned. Definitely a good primer to the world of new ventures, but very repetitive course material.
Ivan is definitely an interesting professor. Students either like him or hate him. He has really good connections in LA and brings amazing speakers to the class. Almost no homework.

Autry is the most arrogant, disorganized professor I have ever taken at USC. Take this class if you are looking for a light workload, don't take it if you are looking to start a new venture.

Autry is an unispiring professor who if very self absored. Most classes, cases, speakers tend to focus around talking about himself or bringing in professionals from the space industry. Nothing to really learn here and seems to be very uninterested in coaching or helping students in a meaninful way on their pitch projects.

The course content is extremely simple and there are no exams, but the professor treats the class like high school students (in the worst way; think the teacher who asked the football team how their game went because he actually does that). Very simple- no exams, just a couple short papers. Professor is condescending and doesn't really teach to our abilities. Not entirely sure what I've gained from this class.

Course material is light - certainly not MBA-level but there are good guest speakers. Professor's personality may be offputting to some. If you are late he makes you sing in front of the class He is not very organized when it comes to what he expects from the assignments.

This course serves a purpose of making entrepreneurship and start-ups more accessible and less daunting. Course was a bit slow but very hands-on and interactive. Professor Glenn Fox was fantastic and would highly reocmmend is other entrepreneurship classes.

Easy class, feels like undergrad-level. High-level intro to entrepreneurship without much that can really be applied to starting a company

Professor is very passionate, great speakers, work load is perfect. You spend the semester bringing one of your ideas to life in the form of a business, which makes it very enjoyable.

This is a great class for anyone interested in launching their own idea, be it a startup, or an idea at a big company.

Great professor! Very caring and you work on any business idea you'd like

Ivan knows his material when it comes to Ecommerce and investing in new ventures. The speakers that came in were also from really cool startups that are very well known. Great class with low workload too
The professor is intense, but in a good way, and the workload is extremely light. The speakers are incredible and you should absolutely take a class with Nikkhoo while at Marshall.

If you are interested in learning more about e-commerce or starting your own e-commerce business take this class. The speakers are really good and provide a lot of insights. Also, I would recommend taking at least one class with Ivan.

I like Ivan, but he is definitely not for everyone. If you don't mind being cold called and in a class environment that is a little bit rash and inappropriate, I would recommend taking it. Ivan is very knowledgeable and brought in amazing speakers that are entrepreneurs in the e-commerce space. This was the first semester the course was offered so I'm sure it will get even better in years to come.

This professor is a bit full of himself and his connections in the entrepreneur community. He is engaging but he doesn't do a good job of communicating key takeaways or clear direction of the course. The guest speaker entrepreneurs are interesting but it would be nice to have some diversity in who he brings in. I thought this course was going to be very useful content but it has fallen short for me.

If you want to learn about e-commerce, this is your class. Ivan knows a lot about the industry and has some great guest speakers, including the CEO of Bouqs.com. He is very well connected in the industry and is able to link the VC space to the entrepreneurship side of things. Very minimal work and grades.

Ivan is a big personality, but he's fun and extraordinarily well connected in the LA investing and entrepreneur ecosystems. He brings in the best guest speakers in Marshall by far. You will learn a ton from all the VCs and founders that come to speak.

The class has minimal work. No real exams and a semster-long group project that is not that difficult.

Ivan brings entrepreneurs to classes to share their entrepreneurial stories, which broadened my horizons. If you are or want to be a person full of curiosity and creativity, this is the elective you should take. How much you can get from this class will depend on how much efforts you put into it. It is a good starting point for entrepreneurship.
one reading-ish per class and 1-3 memos due each week.
Same as above. Pay close attention to the weekly deliverables and syllabus esp flexible assignments

This class has a small deliverable each week but they are pretty low lifts/efforts. The Professor definitely has deep connections to eCommerce and is pretty good at teaching some of the basics. Each topic could probably be covered in more depth, but that's the nature of a survey course like this.
too much busy work and I didn't learn anything neww
Lots of papers, but really great speakers, and opportunity to directly apply lessons to your internship/prior jobs, etc.

Professor is kind of condescending and full of himself. Will bring in a high profile guest speaker and only give them like 20-30 minutes to talk. More busy work than necessary for a class of this nature. Very case-based, discussion wanders and he doesn't tie it all together that much.

This class is just ok, the cases we read are not bad, although we tend to focus on large companies who are not very entrepreneurial such as P&G and IBM which have really struggled in the past decade.  It would be nice to focus on faster growing companies who are innovating successfully.  The Professor likes to have "warm calls" where he will call you down before class starts and asks if you read the case and are prepared to talk about a certain aspect of the case.

The content in this class is really interesting, and I think everyone should be prepared to think like an entrepreneur, even in a corporate environment. However, it's a case-based class and the professor is just really, really bad at managing the classroom environment around case discussions. Rather than encourage an actual authentic conversation, he seems to have an "answer" in mind and really refuses to incorporate any alternative viewpoints that come up in class. I'd say that he fails to create the environment of psychological safety that's required for a case-based class to be really successful.
Readings/cases have been quite interesting and relevant. The professor has a lot of experience as well as contacts and bring in very interesting guest speakers.

The professor brings in some solid speakers from Walmart, Adobe, BMW etc. It's kind of just lecture style rather than conversational so it can feel a little dry at times. The professor has you purchase a bunch of the cases (that he's written) and will talk a lotttt about his McKinsey days. Overall I'd give it a 7/10. Good high level discussions around what is corporate entrepreneurship?, not too much homework besides lots of reading, fairly socratic style teaching.

You have to really engage in the classroom for this one. It's really interesting material, and Jermey Dann facilitates good discussion. But he doesn't bring a ton of energy to the subject matter. The students really need to be invested in the classroom though. Aside from case reading, there is a pretty minimal workload. Incredible speakers. You read a case, and often the protagonist comes to class the next week. Most high level speakers i've seen at Marshall

The professor is brilliant and this is a great class. The class is an interesting mix of MBA students and MSSE and Price students. So MBAs who are not necessarily finance driven will easily be able to handle the finance portion of the class. Additionally since this is an MBA class the professor assumes that students don't know that much about the impact space and makes this portion of the material very approachable. Overall, a very enjoyable class and a great introduction to the impact space - which is growing in importance everyday.
Interesting course if you're passionate about the subject matter, professor tends to assign lots of reading but not all is necessary

Great class. Many students from the Social Entrepreneurship Program take this class so be ready for some very basic finance explanation that may take half of the class time. This tends to get boring but overall the class is great.

She is the real deal. HOWEVER this class is mainly attended by MSSE students, they are an odd bunch. Good to understand startup funding as well as basics of finance in addition to impact investing. She works full time in this field and very up to date about everything. She should be just giving lectures rather than make it a participatory class, oh well.

Professor is smart and a current practitioner in the field, but there are moments you hope he can command the class better, but doesn't. He brings in really great guests and keeps the class engaging. But the content can be rudimentary and the pace slow. There are a number of assignments and skill builders. The skill builders are a great concept - we go through a due diligence memo, a business model canvas, and pro forma forecasts - but we never revisit those tools at all. Most of the students are also in the MSSE program, so you get a nice mix of students.

You can learn a lot about startups, especially in impact investing, from this class. There are guest speakers every class, which gives you great exposure to the material (cases) you read. Also, plenty of employment opportunities through Jennifer and the guest speakers. Really fascinating material and companies that you analyze, but it does get super dry sometimes. Jennifer doesn't let you out early, so you are there throughout the night and that can drag on.
If you're interested in impact investing then this is a good class. Prof Walske is really passionate about the topic and it shows

This class teaches you about term sheets and due diligence. You'll have a semester long project to do due diligence on a real startup for them to have a chance to get a real 50k check. It is a group project and you meet with the founder several times. Apart from that, there's readings and blog posts and activities. The class is not very structured and the syllabus is always changing. The prof really cares and is really interested/animated/knowledgeable.
The only way to get involved in Marshall's Venture Fund program. Class is very easy.
Without a finance background, it is sometimes hard to follow but the class is still manageable and interesting if you're interested in learning about VC at a baseline level

A great class to understand the VC industry and how to be an investor. You actually get to source for and decide what company Marshall Venture Fund should invest in. Very experiential as you have founders come pitch to you and you perform diligence on their companies. You also have industry experts - lawyers, VC, founders - come in to teach you what you need to know

Very disorganized course. Professor does not provide much insight into VC industry, term sheets, etc. Start-ups that present are not typically "investment grade."
 Who is this class for? Someone interested in VC.
 Final Thoughts: Would not recommend unless the course is given more structure. Not much insights gained into the VC world. Mostly lectures about professor's experience and personal anecdotes.

Do not take this course unless you are seriously considering Venture Capital. The speakers are good, class isn't too much work, but the vibe (bit intense) and activities (genuine outreach and relationship management with startups) are a lot if you are not committed to the follow-through. If you want to enter VC, this class is an amazing access point to professionals in the field. Guest professors Jack and Jai are also kind and attentive.

The opportunity to hear from and speak to industry professionals is priceless! However, the other part of the class (managing the Marshall Venture Fund and associated projects/assignments) is frequently unorganized and lacks clarity. Having multiple instructors for the class creates confusion, particularly when the instructors are not all aligned. The VC instructors of the class (Jack Crawford and Jai Choi) are great. Hopefully the details will be ironed out for the next elective cohort. The projects/assignments consist of both individual and group work - it's manageable but does require research tasks and founder outreach/calls.

The Venture Lab is a mixed experience. The biggest value is the instructors and the speakers they bring in: Jack and Jai, both venture GPs and instructors, who bring deep experience, insight, and extensive networks, making them by far the highlight of the course. Hopefully the format will shift so students who actively show up can engage and ask questions, rather than relying on pre-submitted questions based on bios, which are often AI-generated. That would make class time far more valuable.

The team component is brutal. This term, each group picked five companies, but four out of five, for anyone with VC experience, were not venture-backable and appear to be sourced through personal connections. There’s little enforcement around the fund thesis or general clarity on the fund thesis, which amplifies the frustration and makes expectations unclear. Working in teams under these conditions is a major challenge and makes the course feel more academic than practical.

Overall, the class is best suited for two types of students: those seeking first exposure to VC, assuming no prerequisite is required, or students with some VC knowledge who are qualified to participate in a student investment fund that deploys real capital.

Do not take this course unless you are seriously considering Venture Capital. The speakers are good, class isn't too much work, but the vibe (bit intense) and activities (genuine outreach and relationship management with startups) are a lot if you are not committed to the follow-through. If you want to enter VC, this class is an amazing access point to professionals in the field. Guest professors Jack and Jai are also kind and attentive.

I honestly think this should be a required course for MBA students. It focuses on user empathy and user design in innovation, but allows students to experience all that goes into designing and producing a prototype of a product (including the intensive feedback process, high pressure, and emotional roller coasters/investment). This course is by far the most rewarding and most painful class I've taken in the program thus far. Take it as a fair warning: this class requires a lot of time, work, and effort, but well worth it. I wish I could have dedicated a whole semester to this class alone. Abby cares so dearly for her students and for the contents of this course.

This may be one of the most valuable classes I take at Marshall. We learn design thinking methodology and apply it in real life to create solutions for challenges faced by an identified target population in the field. Abby is also a skilled instructor and makes a 3 hour class engaging, which is impressive. I will say this class will ask A LOT of you, so only pursue if you are serious and willing to put in some genuine time and thought work. Also keep in mind this class is almost entirely filled with MSSE students. I am the only MBA in my class.

I think this course would have been so much more dyanmic in person. The virtual space I think hindered this course. The course is mainly made up of Masters of Social Entrepreneurship students and the course takes you through the entire Human-Centered Design process. You work in teams to bring a product to market. Workload is front-load heavy. Students need to conduct 30 meaningful conversations and have to distill findings from there.

This is a great class and the learnings are different from our typical MBA classes. I have enjoyed being able to learn the human centered design approach. However, it is a LOT of work. You need to conduct 30 interviews in the first few weeks.  The class is also mostly comprised of MSSE students who tend to be much younger than MBA students (some are still in undergrad and completing their graduate coursework at the same time) and are very unorganized and inefficient (at least that was my experience with my team). The pace of class time itself is slow and the professor has to hand-hold a lot. Overall I've learned a lot in the class but wouldn't recommend taking during a time you want to be recruiting or have other competing priorities.

This course would've been much better in person, first and foremost. I'm sure the professor would've been able to deliver a much better experience. You should know that the course feels like an intro course to human-centered design and so it's slow and geared towards MSSEs who are in their first semester of grad school, but also comes with a lot of coursework that you really can't avoid doing or find shortcuts for. I would suggest this course if you are TRULY interested in social entrepreneurship and social impact and you have the time in the rest of your schedule to take this on.
Easy class, interesting content
Have to go to class and its easy class
Prof Fox is definitely in the top 10 Marshall faculty. Take any / every class available that he teaches, especially this class.

I don't think 1.5 credit classes are very valuable to begin with (either too little content or way too much that it should be a 3 credit class). This one falls on the little side. Very manageable from a workload perspective and Sherry is very nice (albeit a bit unorganized) but if you've worked in the media/entertainment field then none of the content will likely be new to you. It could be a nice refresher for prepping with interviews and if you're not familiar with the space then it does coiver the major trends nicely.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: Professor Sherry has amazing experience in the film, TV, animation, CPG & Ed Tech industries. Her classes bring in guest speakers from some of these fields so it is a great networking opportunity. The class also offers opportunities to create a pitch for your own start-up and improve it along the way. Course work is very light and the professor is flexible. It's a very good 1.5 credit class for people interested in understanding the entrepreneurial mindset in the entertainment industry. The only downside is that you may not find a lot of value add if you're interested in Sports, Music or Gaming.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: If you are interested in learning more about the entertainment space, Professor Sherry has many connections and brings in several speakers to share their stories and advice in the industry. The work is very doable. A few papers and a final presentation. It was a great class and she often invites students to have dinner with the speakers to establish relationships.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: Great class not only to gain insight on the evolving industry of entertainment but also the entrepreneurial opportunities that exist within the industry.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: Very good speakers. The project could be a bit more specific and relevant. The professor is a good connection to have if you are into entertainment.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

career: Leadership Role in Entertainment or Financial Services
comments: Great speakers and lectures. Class is engaging and content is relevant and interesting.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: This class is split between lectures on the recent history of the Entertainment industry, a few guest speakers, and a team project where you come up with a new venture and pitch the class. Prof has an amazing background in kids animation and is generous with her knowledge and leveraging contacts to bring in equally cool guests. The lectures are hit or miss - if you know the industry you won't learn anything new. The team project is fun and the q&a with classmates is brutal but helpful.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: Enjoyable course. Great guest speakers from the industry. Innovative. very Manageable workload.
topic_title: BAEP 575 - Entrepreneurship in the Media and Entertainment Industry

comments: Interesting class. Professor makes it engaging. The class covers many interesting topics about tech commercialization and strategy for entrepreneurs.
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments: Nice to actually have an entrepreneurship professor with start-up experience, as opposed to an academic. This makes the teaching actionable instead of theoretical
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments: Chill class. Better than those fluffy MOR classes.
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments: Easy class. 4 memo papers and final paper. It's more like a leadership class and based on the certain topic discussion
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments: This class and professor are fantastic. Geraldine has real-world experience, and the class feels fruitful. There is minimal reading and few assignments, but more so, it feels like a useful class to talk about successful and flawed businesses. I definitely recommend.
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments:
The course is fairly easy without much workload. The assignments are also easy to do, including the group assignments. 
Who is this class for? Anyone interested in starting a new venture, or who wants to work in a startup can take this. It helps go through the various team building issues that a founder can face, including building culture, layoffs etc.
Final Thoughts: More real life cases could have been helpful. Currently we go through slides which is not as engaging.
topic_title: BAEP 577 - The Entrepreneurial CEO: The Real World of Leading Startups

comments: So this class is a little complicated. It's hard to measure without considering the professor because he didn't use a syllabus and his assignments were kinda designed as the seminar went on. He splits his classes in two: first half are going over your questions on the articles you read in advance of class (brutal), and the second half is a guest speaker entrepreneur friend of his (interesting to great depending on the speaker). So, it's a little hit or miss. Easy A and light work, but I might have gone a different route if it worked with my schedule.

Paul is one of a kind. He is anti-education and there are a lot of WTF moments, but in the end, I think we're going to be better off having been his presense for 8 weeks. This is an easy class in terms of workload. It really is all about adjusting your mindset to think like an owner. Due to COVID-19, we are missing out on Paul's genoristy (he usually buys dinner every week and also invites the class to his home in Santa Barbara).

Loved this class. Paul is quite the character, you spend the first hour and a half just asking questions about the articles you read and you have to ask them in a way he likes. There are no exams. You get dinner in class and there are guest speakers. I really enjoyed this class but you have to be okay with being a little uncomfortable.
Less focused on entrepreneurship and more focused on current events. The class was intimate and engaging and definitely non-traditional (in a good way).
Taking the class with Paul is genuniely an incredible experience. Although the class itself is a bit unorthodox, you learn so much and Paul is a great professor. Plus the free dinners are great!

This class is a vibe. There are no exams or even a syllabus. Each week the professor emails a ton of news articles to read and submit your questions on them. He hasn't explained the reason for it but he sits us all in a circle and there's a rapidfire round where everyone asks questions. If the Prof thinks its a good question, he'll give you a sticker. Notetaking is discouraged. But there's free food.
This class will give you a very new experience.
Best class in Marshall

Although there is not much actual work, this class can be extremely difficult for those who don't like to talk in class - it forces you to get over your fear of being cold called and having to think on the spot. So not as much academic work technically, but you have to be 1000000% on in class.
Who is this class for? Someone who either wants to get over their fear of public speaking, or someone who loves public speaking and thinking on their feet, or truly just anyone in general - EVERYONE at Marshall should take this class
Final Thoughts: This is by far the best course I've taken at Marshall. Paul is quirky but truly amazing and so wise and I can't believe how lucky I was to have the opportunity to share space with and learn from him.

career: Entertainment | Entertainment - creator economy or social media
comments: Who is this class for? Students open to learning about entrepreneurship or already know they want to be an entrepreneur
The course prepares you to be a better public speaker. No notes allowed and you are put on the spot to ask better questions and make better comments as course sessions progress.

This was the best class I've ever taken. Paul was amazing and I actually learned so much about how to think and go about the world. There are some learnings from this class that I'll carry with me forever.

Paul challenges you to think about things you don't typically focus on. I am no entrepreneur, but from talking to some of the guest speakers they have been so inspiring. Forces you to think about becoming more wordly aware and ready to anticipate problem solving business problems. You need to bid a lot of points for this class.

By far the most beneficial course at USC. Paul doesn’t believe in taking notes or tests, but rather fostering conversations about real news and how it impacts your life, no matter what industry you want to go in.
Paul says some wacky things and can definitely make you uncomfortable, but there is no class that prepares you better for public speaking and to ask important questions at Marshall than this one.
Class has no work. Interesting to hear Paul's perspective on various topics
Teaching style is absolutely amazing! Best class I've taken in my life. Period.

"Fantastic opportunity to learn about a different way of solving social and business problems. The only draw back is that it is a night class. It also has a lot of students from different programs which can cut both ways at times 
"
Easy class not sure if it will be offered again. Very unbusiness school like in a good way
Inspiring professor. Sometimes classes got a little redundant, however he brought in great speakers and getting learning about the world of social enterprises was refreshing.
great introduction to business frameworks in the social impact space. Very moving speakers. Mid-term is lousy and feels like an undergraduate exam/does not add any value to experience

The professor really cares about the students and is very accessible. The class is almost completely case-based but it does require a lot of work. It is more of a consulting class that happens to only discuss environmental cases than a truly environmentally sustainable class. The teacher provides an excellent framework for attacking issues that would be helpful for almost anyone in any field but it does get repetitive. If this is a half semester class I would recommend it to most people, if it is a full semester class it probably makes more sense for students very interested in the subject area or those who are pursuing the environmental sustainable certificate.
Very interesting guest lecturers, relatively easy assignments and tests

The class is comprised of weekly guest speakers who are involved in various roles within social entrepreneurship. The class focuses on learning about the growing field as opposed to starting an actual social enterprise, so just be aware of that.

The class starts off really strong; great guest speakers... but at some point starts to fizzle out. The midterm was cancelled like two days before b/c we didn't have enough material. A softer class; but also useful to realize that business is not all about the bottom line, and a company can do good and make a profit too
Big name speakers almost every class, panel of alumni, great mix of powerpoint and activities. Only midterm and final, as well as a group project. Must attend class, but it is well worth it!

Unless you have a burning passion for Social Entrepreneurship this class is awfully dry and boring. Professor speaks for a good hour and a half. There are often guest speakers in class who sometimes are passionate and engaging and interesting, but others who are just as dry. There is minimal engagement in class.
The speakers in this class are amazing - they are helping me think about how to structure a social enterprise in the future.

Favorite class all year! If you've always wanted to change the world, "but don't know how", TAKE THIS CLASS. /  / Professor Wertman is awesome! He teaches AND shows how you can go into an industry that you care about because it makes a difference. The speakers he brings in are incredibly passionate and come from various backgrounds and experiences.

This course had us work through developing a new social venture that students in the course were actually pursuing or planning to pursue post-MBA. This professor is extremely open and provided dinner for every class! This class also attracts non-MBAs, which provides a diverse set of skills in group work.

Project-focused course that is probably particularly useful for students who have a social venture idea they want to explore. For those without a specific idea, the course addresses some of the key differences between traditional and social entrepreneurship. I was surprised (positively) at how little overlap there was between this class and more traditional BAEP classes. Professor is very well connected, brings in good speakers, and has great resources for those interested in social entrepreneurship.

I would have preferred to take the course under Adlai Wertman honestly. The class under Jill was more like a social venture initiation class than a course about social entrepreneurship. But Jill is kind and brings in great speakers!
Fine class. Pretty laid back, not a ton of work, Jill brings dinner every week. Not as useful/interesting as I'd hoped but probably worth taking if you're big on social impact.

Jill is nice and provides dinner each night, which is the real and only highlight of this class. Overall, however, it is very unfocused and lacks real direction. There is no real insight provided, as she tends to just talk high level and read slides for three hours straight. It is also run like an intro to new ventures class, with very little to differentiate it or dive deep into the social side of business.

I didn't really learn anything new in this class. There was very little organization/structure and the professor tends to ramble a lot. It's targetted for MSSE students so the content felt slightly more basic.
BEST CLASS ON CAMPUS.  Greg Sachs is a LEGEND.  Please beg  to have him come back.  He is a game changer that actually helped Students get jobs.  Incredible experience.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Entrepreneurship in Alternative Asset Management

comments: Fantastic course. Interesting subject about the practical concerns of starting a hedge fund. But what really made the course amazing was the personal involvement of the professor. He really got to know each one of us. Amazing experience!
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Entrepreneurship in Alternative Asset Management

comments: Prof. Sachs is great. Makes class interesting and makes an effort to help each student in their career search.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Entrepreneurship in Alternative Asset Management

comments: The class has great potential. The speakers that Sherry brought were amazing. If you're interested in entertainment it could be of great value to you. Sherry herself is very nice, experienced and flexible. She is a bit monotonic as a speaker, but her connections make up for that. / The only thing that was difficult to me was that it was a Thursday night 6.30-9.30 class, but I guess schedules change :)
topic_title: BAEP 599 - Entrepreneurship in Media & Entertainment Industry
BAEP 599 - Entrepreneurship in Media & Entertainment Industry

comments: The professor had really interesting contacts in the industry; however, the class was run extremely poorly.  She was forced to cut off several excellent speakers due to poor time management during the first half of the course.  Feedback received on assignments was hit and miss as well.  Although this was an "entrepreneurship" class, she provided very little actionable insights other than "network."  Most of the lecture sections were from powerpoint.
topic_title: BAEP 599 - Entrepreneurship in Media & Entertainment Industry

comments: The professor, material, and work all unfortunately felt a waste. Sherry is a very bright industry representative, but success as an entertainment entrepreneur does not easily translate into a worthwhile class. Speakers were mixed and the structure made little sense based on the "learnings."
topic_title: BAEP 599 - Entrepreneurship in Media & Entertainment Industry

comments: Great guest speakers every class but too generalized of lecture content by professor
topic_title: BAEP 599 - Entrepreneurship in Media & Entertainment Industry

comments: You get to assess and conduct due diligence on a real startup in LA, and propose whether the investment committee can make an investment. Great speakers.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Great practical learning working with USC-founded Startups. Workload is relatively light; weekly blog post and a final due diligence memo. Class is mostly comprised of great guest speakers from the VC space.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: the most hands-on course i've taken at Marshall. students conduct diligence on a company and produce an investment memo at the end of the course. michael is very knowledgeable and has lots of connections
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Learned VC relevant stuff from guest speakers and hands-on due dilligence. Pherhaps due to the pandemic, comversations with founders are not smooth and team work is hindered.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Learned VC relevant tools thanks to hands-on due dilligence. The class has guest speakers almost every week, but they are not always relevant - I wish they were more senior sometimes. Perhaps in person these connections are more relevant.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Michael is incredibly thoughtful about the class speakers he brings in, who represent all stages of VC financing. He takes a lot of care in curating founders and startups for students to work with and run due diligence for and provides real-life experience in deciding whether Marshall should invest. Michael also just cares a lot about his students learning and clearly just wants the experience to be valuable, and it 100% is! Highly recommend if you have any interest in VC, no background or experience required!
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Cool guest speakers, definitely a fluffy class but the two professors who taught last spring are great
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Performance Mindset for Business

comments:
Hands on experience conducting due diligence on startups that the venture fund is considering investing in. This is the real deal. 2-3 startups per semester are chosen and presented to the investment committee consisting of some of the most experience venture capitalists in LA and the Bay.

Guest speakers are top-tier. This class offers the most practical application at Marshall.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: Cool guest speakers, definitely a fluffy class but the two professors who taught last spring are great
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Performance Mindset for Business

comments: This class is focused on learning how to analyze a startup and eventually make a recommendation to the Marshall Venture Fund on whether or not to invest in the company your team is working with. Professor Rivera is very hands-off and lets the teams essentially work at their own pace. The class is very unstructured, so be prepared to potentially have big deadlines come up fairly quickly because teams may procrastinate on either working with their company or working on the due diligence until much later in the semester, close to when the large investment paper is due. Additionally, Professor Rivera brings in some great guest speakers from the VC industry, those class sessions tend to be good. Overall, if you're interested in a career in VC or just want to learn about VC in general, I would recommend this class.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: The classes' whole shtick is that most BAEP classes focus on the starutp side while this is one of the few that focus on the VC's perspective. Professor is very knowledgable in the space and brings in amazing guest speakers. You essentially evaluate one startup across the semester and do due diligence during it. Very cool class.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: This class is all about binging speakers in, very good ones. You get a chance to meet them and an opportunity to be able to create a relationship with them. Also, the experience of working with a foudner and analyzing his/her venture is priceless. This class is a must if you want to be in VC or an entrepreneur.
topic_title: BAEP 599 Special Topics: Venture Fund Lab

comments: If you are interested in venture capital or entrepreneurship, then I would recommend this class. The main project involves doing due diligence for an early-stage company that the USC Marshall Venture Fund may invest in. There are exciting guest speakers in most lectures, and Michael Rivera is laid back and very knowledgeable. comments:
This course does not include any exams and is entirely based on regular assignments. While this structure could be beneficial in theory, I found the grading to be quite unfair.
 Who is this class for? This class might be more suitable for students who already have a background in family businesses, especially those whose parents run a company. However, I would not recommend this course for international students. Based on my experience, international students tended to receive significantly lower grades, and it was unclear how the grading criteria accounted for different perspectives or backgrounds.
 Final Thoughts: Overall, I had a disappointing experience with this course.
 
 First, the course was extremely unorganized. Several guest speakers that were announced never showed up, and the professor seemed unfamiliar with Brightspace, which caused a lot of confusion—especially with the last few assignments.
 
 Second, the professor rarely responded to emails. This wasn’t just my personal experience; other students mentioned the same issue, which made it hard to seek clarification or support.
 
 Third, the grading felt unfair and unclear. I attended every class and actively participated along with another Asian female student, yet both of us received only a B. Meanwhile, some local students who was frequently absent received an A. We found this deeply unfair and discouraging.
 
 Future students should be aware that grading may not reflect effort or participation, and communication with the instructor can be very limited.
