It's a 3 hour night class where roughly 2/3 of the time is spent on dumb presentations and uninspiring cases that no one reads until you're asked to answer questions about them.  Deliverables almost every week.  Midterm was an absolute joke.  Seriously, don't take this class.

*High workload*, but high value class. Based on older peer evaluations, I would say this class's value highly depends on the professor. Mohammed is an engaged and passionate prof that wants to make sure that you learn. He's also receptive to feedback.

It's great to atleast have a working knowledge of SQL, Python, Tableau in current business scenario. This course provides it all. It's also STEM. Prof is incredibly invested into making sure you derive value from the course. But I definitely would not recommend the course if not for the Professor.

Great class to learn Python, gephi, tableau, SQL. It is also part of STEM certification. The professor runs fast and relies on help session to teach you the tools and programs. The HWs are time consuming. This class doesn't have exams.
I come from a tech background and have done a lot of analytics work in the past, so no real value-add here. I learnt more in data science class than in this class.

The professor is very kind and patient with students who are not the most knowledgeable and is an engaging speaker. This course is in a weird spot because it tries to cater to both those who know analytics to some level and those who don't. Aside from the first assignment there isn't a lot of homework.

This is kind of an odd course because it combines very general "why does data matter" type material with very specific skills (Python, Gephi, R, etc). The workload isn't too heavy and there are no exams, which is nice. A lot of class time is spent going over how to run code I know I will never apply in "real life" and will not be tested on, but I guess it's kind of nice to have a general sense of what someone more specialized might do. Probably not technical enough if you are a very technical person, and probably too technical for others.

The professor is engaging and tries to maintain a balance between learning specific skills and learning to develop a business mindset and ask the whys. The course load feels like a bit much though for someone who is trying to learn these skills for the forst time

The professor is very engaging and tries his best to cater to everyones different skill levels. However, he does go pretty fast through the code. Agreed with the comment that it's not technical enough for a technical person but too technical for a non-technical person.

It was more like a case discussion class. The professor was nice and tried to be engaging but did not really teach technical skills in the course. You have to learn by yourself since his pace was really fast in class. What's worse was that he did not follow his syllabus and I had a hard time finding specific topics in the recordings.

Took this course to learn some data modeling in R but spent most of the time durimg case reviews which is not a point of the DSO class. The professor is a nice person but she is new,hence has limited idea about what is the appropriate workload. We have 4 case review assignments that each take 4-5 hours to complete, 2 exams and 2 group projects (5 deliverables each). Not worth the effort. Very limited learning!
If you are interested in learning Python, this class helps. That said you do not need to use python to get through the class, just excel.

A useful course, a bit of a disadvantage being that my class session is on Saturday mornings. The course is worth taking and the professor was excellent in allowing flexibility with Zoom sessions, etc. The professor is an industry professional and brings his learnings into the course often. The structure is a bit confusing but the Analytic Solver applications are great.

It is somewhat of a catchall course for Analytics. It attemps to brush along most techniques that are standard in an analytics toolbox. This particular one was offered online on Saturday mornings, hence seemed to be popular with Online/PT MBA folks. Dasgupta started off with a lot of passion, but it tempered a bit later, perhaps matching the energy of the class... He knows his stuff though, and is very experienced with on-the-ground analytics problems, especially in supply chain, logistics, operations, and the like. One thing to keep in mind when selecting which instructor to take the course with is the tool they will use to teach it. Dasgupta taught it with this add-on to Excel called Frontline Solver, which is insanely easy to use, but think about whether you will have access to it in the environment you will work in. It makes for a great foundation to take other DSO courses, and is requisite for the certificate. Dasgupta is a kind soul, makes the class fun (as much as it could be in an online setting), and is very approachable, while taking the class serious. It can be an easy A.

Tathagata Dasgupta is a great instructor and he is very engaging. Out of the 
10 zoom sessions that we have had, there have only been 2 ocassions in which I felt that I 
didn't learn anything. Sometimes he goes through slides a bit quickly; but it is easy to
teach yourself the material given that his slides are highly organized and have very useful content.
The first midterm was very doable and the HW is very manageable given that it is worth 20%. In
addition, his TA has been very helpful and is an active participant in our learning.
Professor is good but dry and 3 hours on a Tuesday night can be brutal.  It useful class that introduces you to lots of tools
This class is for you who want to know the core of business analytics without too technical lesson

I'd say this class is actually very important for those pursuing a professional career because it teaches, in general, how to collect, process, and present data. However, the class feels unstructured, and the assignments are sometimes unclear and change from time to time. If this can be improved, it could become an interesting class. The quiz, exam, and assignment workload is probably between easy and moderate.
Great professor. This is a good class to improve excel skills and dealing with data. Somewhat too theoretical, but eventually gets there in terms of practicality.
The course is geared more to students studying for PhD in the field, less what would be relevant to an MBA. It is a new course, so she plans to rework based on feedback.

This class is too theoretical, and the professor has made few attempts to make it useful for MBAs. If you want to deep-dive into probability and learn a bit of calculus, without knowing how to apply it, only then go for it!
You should only take this class if you want to be a statistician and you are very good with numbers
Way too mathematical and in the weeds.

class was solid in that it covered modeling scenarios.  It got a bit technical at times, which rubbed some students the wrong way.  But in Amy's defense, you can't just teach students how to press a button for a model without understanding the underlying mechanics.

The class was new this year -- hopefully it will be reformulated to make it more applicable.  As it was, it was dry and esoteric will little examples to tie in-class concepts to real-world application.

This was the first time this class has been offered so it may change in the future. Be warned!  You need to have a decent Calculus background though. If you don't remember how to do integrals and differentials, then you better take a refresher course.  It's a lot of theory.  The practical application of this class seems to be low.
I didn't find this information terribly useful.  She overcomplicated concepts while teaching.  I'm still not sue how to implement what I learned.

Good class to understand the basics of probability and minimal data modeling. Class is really easy and expectations are pretty low. Nonetheless, a good class to get your feet wet in Data Analysis and Modeling.

I was a bit disappointed with this course but I that was more due to the professor than the content. Amy Ward is very nice but she didn't really communicate the material in a business sense. It was very heavy on complex statistics jargon.

This is not a class for MBAs. This is only useful for people trying to become analysts/business analytics students. Amy moves too fast and the course itself is mostly useless. The class averaged a 47% on the final.

It's just another data class, but professor Ward, although very thoughtful with the students, wasn't born to be a professor. She just made everyone more confused about data modeling. The slides are terrible and the class is too unstructured. I would suggest to take another data class! The only problem is that this class is required for Monte Carlo Simulation (another one I won't take, because of professor Ward) =/

The class could possibly be useful, however the professor cannot instruct her way out of a cardboard box. Nonetheless, never going to class, putting in minimal effort to the homework, and getting a 30% on the final will still get you a B+.

This course is difficult if you are not quantitatively inclined. Prof. Ward is not great at explaining difficult concepts--her heart is definitely in the right place, and she's enthusiastic about the subject matter, but the execution isn't always there. The final was quite difficult and the curve was strong. All that being said, I definitely learned some useful material, particularly around Monte Carlo simulations. Overall, I'd recommend it, but only if you plan to go into data analytics, product management, or maybe finance.

This course helped expand my thinking around uncertainty in the business world and modeling risk. I now feel more comfortable starting from scratch in answering questions like "How many customers would want to purchase this non-existent product?"
teaches necessary analytical skills & modelling, but pace of the course is too fast. professor teaches at the speed of light. would get a lot more out of the class if it was a full semester course.

Lots of useful information in this class that you don't realize at first. Great intro to modeling data if you're new to it. Very approachable. Dawn is lovely and patient with students. Highly recommend taking earlier than later.

Dawn is amazing and she does a good job at trying to cram a lot of info into a 1.5 credit class. She goes FAST though and because it's such a short class you don't get a lot of time to digest the information. Relatively light workload but enough to make you actually learn by hand.
Dawn is a great teacher!
If you do not have a good understanding of statistics, this class is great. If you do, this will be just a review.

Dawn is a great professor but the course is just so fast that it's difficult to learn and retain information. You go over a lot quickly (some of it is very interesting) but the application of it is hard to determine since you're constantly adding new information.
The class is very applied and hands-on, and Professor Porter is very approachable.

Porter is great - very knowledgable, funny, engaging, and patient. This class was a great overview of different distributions and issues in probability. I'm curious to learn more and sad that I didn't have enough room to add her monte carlo class.
The class starts from very basics of Probability and covers some advanced topics such as simulations, different distributions and teaches some important excel skills.
Class picks up in difficulty and pace given time constraints. Professor Porter is awesome.

Class starts with basic probability and quickly becomes very difficult and dense.  The class is mostly MS Analytics students who have much more experience with this kind of coursework.  Grades are mostly determined by homework assignments which are fairly difficult, followed by an open book final exam.

If you do not know Python, do not take this class. This class changed a professor this semester and Professor Pollok structured this class heavily around Python. This class is extremely quant heavy, but to be fair it is right there in the name. The professor is pretty decent at explaining, but very dry and the concepts are challenging. If Kristen Chenowith became a stats teacher, she would be Dawn Porter. Fantastic teacher who really cares about her students. The material is incredibly dry and difficult, but if you're interested in practical application of regression, this is the class for you.

This class is indeed advanced. The concepts are difficult and the analyses are technical. The class relies on JMP software, which is a lighter version of SAS. If you want to do any sort of predictive analytics, this class is probably one you should take. Be ready to pay attention, as it would be hard to complete the take-home exams if you had to relearn how to do everything then.

The class is great.  It can get pretty confusing but she doesn't go too fast and adjusts if she can tell that no one is understanding.  The material is super useful if you are going to do any type of data analysis regardless of function or industry.  Highly recommend this one.
Professor Porter dubms down high technical concepts. She combines lecture and lab sessions so whatever your learning preference is you'll get it.

Professor Porter is excellent! The content can get prety complex and the course is fast paced, but the professor is very good. Exams are "take home", so another benefit of this class is that it is less stressful because you can take your time to answer test questions.

Dawn Porter is one of the best professors at Marshall. I am eager to use the concepts learned in this class specifically in my summer internship. She made the material very relevant to business and is a very fun teacher.

This is great for anyone who thinks is going to be using data analytics in their career. Dawn has a great way of teaching and organizes the class to make it easy on students. Highly recommend this class!

Not sure how much I'll actually use regression in the real world but it's a great course to learn a data analysis software (JMP) and get into the quant mindset.

Professor Porter is really nice, course has a pretty light workload, exams are take-homes.

Professor Porter is really great, especially in this class. Professor Porter also really cares about her students and will pause to answer any questions. She also answers them in-depth to ensure everyone understands what's being taught. Would highly recommend this class and this professor.

If you liked Dawn's GSBA 524 class then you will be able to handle this class. Same teaching style, more advanced regressions. You do not use R, but JMP. Super intuitive platform. Class assignments are group homeworks and a take home midterm and final. Very fair grading and assignments.

This class is NOT a natural progression to the MBA Data Science course, although it is supposed to be. If you come only from that course, the course might surprise you in its depth. It needs a much stronger handle on statistical analysis than the core course or even other application based analytics course. Dawn is as always, a great instructor. The course delves deeper into real world analyses for each of the regression techniques: simple/ols/multiple/weighted least squares, time series, etc. Assignments can feel hard but grading is probably lenient. Dawn makes it easy to understand, but expect to put in your own work to understand stats if you want to be theoritically sound. If not, it will give anyone who will do this kind of work enough practical tools. Sessions are recorded, attendance is not tracked (but I recommend going), assignment cadence is light.

Some of the coursework seems like it would be useful if I could actually put it into practice, but it's been incredibly tough to follow what's been going on so far. This course seems to be designed to be delivered to math majors, as >50% of the lecture slides are are just full of equations without any guidance on how or when to implement them in a business setting. Some of the data techniques seem like they could conceivably be useful in certain business situations, but I can't really imagine how I would implement them in a real-world setting, nor would I feel comfortable doing so with my limited understanding of the techniques we've covered (my experience in consulting so far is limited to a big 4 summer internship, so take this with a grain of salt). The expectation seems to be that you will need to go to his office hours to actually understand what's going on, which is a teaching practice that I disagree with entirely. 

Paat is a fun guy but I really feel like >90% of the class has no idea what they're doing right now. He really needs to start with simpler concepts and build upon them progressively rather than diving right into advanced probabilities and modeling. Before the mid-term he told us 'I have to put in questions where you can copy/paste from the spreadsheets I give you, otherwise half the class would get a zero.' I don't think anyone actually finished the mid-term. Unless you are going really data-heavy, most people are probably better off taking the Spreadsheets for Business class instead (just probably not with Rogers).
topic_title: DSO 570 - The Analytics Edge: Data, Models, and Effective Decisions

Paat is a really great professor, he makes the class.  Even though its been difficult and a major time suck, I think I will benefit in the long run from having taken this class.

The topics are interested and the professor is very knowledgeable. However, I feel this class is designed for students in the Supply Chain Management Program only (I would say that less than 20% of the class is comprised by MBA students). It is strongly focused on detailed calculations and specific concepts/definitions instead of developing your problem solving skills (In terms of the tests). As for the projects, assignments and readings they are interesting and useful to develop your ability to approach problems in the real life.
Slightly hard and class was not terribly interesting but material was extremely useful for ops & supply chain related fields

The class is very data-driven. There's a lot of work every week but readings and assignments provide a great learning experience for those interested in supply chain / operations. The professor was a bit monotonous but the good content beats her presentation skills. I think the course is highly underestimated by many.
Very useful class if youre interested in operations/supply chain management. Professor is very kind.

The class content is fine, it teaches a very high level view of various supply chain concepts. If you want a review of this and lack industry experience this would be a good class. The professor is knowledgable but not engaging.
Class has quite a lot of homework. Good mix of cases and theory, can be a little dry at times. A bit of overlap with the Operations core class.

Useful content but very boring and so much work. There are 4 individual papers, 4 group papers, 4 individual HW assignmnents, a midterm, a final, and a final presentation. This is way too much work. Wishes he would break down the math concepts more. Interesting cases.
Class has quite a lot of homework. Good mix of cases and theory, can be a little dry at times. A bit of overlap with the Operations core class.

Same professor from our MBA core class - Operations so I am familiar with the teaching style and the course design. The class also accomodates many Master students so the class material is very specific to supply chain issues; a certain degree of overalp with core class but a good addition if your future role ever requires collab or understanding of supply chain.

topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: I like Raman, but the class is way way too simple. I feel like it's an undergrad 101 level class, where we touch on various subjects within service management. I don't think I really learned anything here.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: The topic is queuing, wait times and optimum pricing- so if you're not interested in working in a service business than you won't enjoy this course. The course is very data heavy which is good if you want to get a better grasp on regression models and excel.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: If you intend on working in the service industry (from retail to finance to education), you should consider this course. The professor is humorous, engaging, and clearly cares for us, the students.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: This should be a core class. It teaches many vital business theories and practical applications. The professor is quite interactive and innovative in his teaching style. Cases are short, succinct, and effective.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: This is one of the best designed and best thought-out classes I've had in my entire academic career. The readings are carefully curated and do not take a lot of time to complete, but provide tremendous value and insight into the management and operations of a services firm. This is one of those classes where you WANT to do the reading because you know it will be interesting, engaging, and informative.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments: Every class has a specific subject and 1-2 takeaways at the end. Very to-the-point. Readings are carefully picked so that you don't spend too much time on them but get the most out of them. There are not many MBAs in the class if you care about your classmates. That may make the experience too easy because many of the students are medical students who don't even know Excel. A bit data heavy which is good. The class drives the thought process.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments:
Course content is different from what was delivered in core and not covered (even remotely) by many of the other electives. The content is very useful, even if you are not going into Operations as a career function. Course is a mix of case reading and practical applications (in Excel).
 
 The professor is very good at delivering the content, which is relevant to today's business problems.
topic_title: DSO 582 - Service Management: Economics and Operations

comments:
Useful class. Interesting projects.
Multipel homeworks and deliverables.
Not very difficult. Excel a bit.

This class is a lot of work but you learn a lot from it and it's great for people interested in operations or for people interested in working on a real project for a company. Bayiz is awesome and really cares about the students and he helps up be successful in our projects.

Very useful class that help understand consulting industry better and provide an opportunity to practice consulting. I really like different techniques that are taught in class. Could be very helpful for people who are interested in this area or not sure if they want to go into this area.

Prof. Bayiz is awesome. However, having taken Project Management with him before, in comparison, Ops Consulting seems lacking in actual content to some extent. But it's great exposure working on the live industry consulting project. Also, lots of small assignments/HW in this class.
The project makes or breaks this class. You get a good overview of Ops Consulting and frameworks. Very practical and relatively easy. The project can take a lot of time.

This is a class in which every student will be assigned to a client project. The projects are challenging, and give the student a real life experience on how to service the client's business challenges. Excellent class for those interested in consulting. He teaches Visio, and cases related to consulting. Highly 3ed.
The project makes or breaks this class. You get a good overview of Ops Consulting and frameworks. Very practical and relatively easy. The project can take a lot of time.

The content is highly useful for future professional skills, not only for consultancy but also for any customer-facing or project-based positions. The professor is super nice and easy-to-communicate. This class is highly recommenced for people interested in consulting, product management, project management, and internal strategic planning.
Project selected will really make or break this class. Bayiz is awesome but a non-engaging project will limit enjoyment of this class.

Bayiz is funny, interesting and seems to genuinely care about his students. He also provides good instruction with regard to skills that are actually marketable in a professional environment. 

You'll actually get to work on a consulting engagement with some interesting clients such as Northrop Grumman, TOMS, Nestle, J&J etc. There are a lot of projects across a variety of fields. If you're looking to be a consultant this is a a must take class.
Nice project during the semester

Tableau and powerpoint exercises were very useful for consulting fields; decent amount of work is required since the majority of the work is a client facing consulting project (good choice of companies & projects to choose from)

Take before your internship if you're going into consulting and haven't done consulting ppt slides before. Helps you visualize data, which is great for everyone. Bayiz is awesome and the work load isn't too much. The major project kind of sucks but no worse than any other class.

Professor is awesome - humourous and helpful. Class content is very practical and really puts you in the shoes of a consultant. No exams but a consulting project with actual clients with weekly/bi-weekly client discussions. Practical skills learned in class include Excel (PivotTables), Visio and Tableau.

Strongly recommend for those interested in operations and/or operations consulting. Great practical skills including Excel, Visio, Tableau, all with a focus on building effective consulting results/presentations. Project based class where the value you get back from the project probably varies somewhat from project to project. Wish I had taken this class prior to my operations internship. Class is a high workload class, so balance with lighter classes, but definitely worth the effort for those entering these fields.

Professor Bayiz is nice. The software traning sessions are very slow and basic, so don't expect to learn great excel, powerpoint, visio, etc from him. Interesting guest speakers (all from consulting firms; Deloitte, PWC,...). 40% of the course grade is from a group project, where you have a real world "consulting style" problem to solve for a company (J&J, TOMS, Nestle,...). There are 3 class presentations for this project + all the presentations and meetings with the client. This project can be very time consuming (or not, depends on your group). If you want to go into consulting specifically for Operations, it is a must take course. Otherwise, it is not so great.

This class provides a great learning experience because it gives you the opportunity to use tools that are widely applied in the industry, you get access to real life problems through the consulting project you work on (it's hands-on with real data and with a clearly defined goal (more than PRIME), you practice continually with short exercises to force you to learn the tools and topics.

You use:
- MS Visio
- Excel Solver
- Tableau

You get real life projects with companies like: Nestle, J&J, Tom's, etc.

The professor is well organized and has a clear structure for the course with very helpful reminders of the weekly schedule on Sundays.
Murat is one of the best professors. The class is project based but you will still learn Visio, Tableu and practice creating decks.

The class will be useful for both consultants and non-consultants. You'll learn ppt skills, Tableau, Visio, presentation skills. You will work on a real consulting project which may take a lot of time. Otherwise the workload is not huge.

This is my second class with Bayiz. He is very nice, has a great personality, and cares lot that you are learning and getting a useful experience. You will learn some valuable programs like Tableau, Visio, etc. that are tangible takeaways and will conduct an actual operations consulting project for a company. I think what you put into it will be what you get out of it. My criticism of the course is that there are too many guest speakers who just about all are from the consulting world and it becomes too repetitive (especially since attendance is "mandatory" for guest speaker days).
This is the most effective instructor in the MBA program. The class directly provides students with hard resume skills regardless of career field, specifically in Visio, Excel, & Tableau.

I took Prof. Bayiz's project management class before this one. I liked the structure of project management more than this one. While I believe the real-world consulting project will be helpful, I didn't care for the structure of the class. You learn useful tools such as Tableau and Visio but I found that 20% of class time was wasted on housekeeping items such as lecturing us on how to dress/how to write e-mails to clients. If you're interested in ops consulting, I would take this.

You learn useful skills within excel, tableau, and powerpoint. Guest speakers are every week or two, and they are great. You also choose a project in which you are to help their operations as if you are a consulting team. Workload is managable, with very few assigned readings.

There are good basic/practical skills you learn in this class that make it worthwhile but the consulting project is time consuming/not worthwhile so be aware. You will learn Excel and PPT tricks, Tableau, Visio and important Ops calculations/appraoches to problem solving. Prof Bayiz is fun and lighthearted, VERY organized and always makes sure that every student is caught up before advancing in content--he genuinely cares.

I took this class to get a hands-on learning experience with a real world operations problem, so to that extent, the class has fulfilled that. However, I'm not sure it gives us the tools to actually solve said problem since we are working with ops experts and we as students have very little ops experience. If you're not going into consulting, the guest lectures can be pretty dull. The professor does care about the students, but I'm not sure I'd take this class if I had the chance to pick again.

This course is very useful for learning more about how to construct a PowerPoint, formatting data in Excel and Tableau and learning how to use Visio - all very useful skills for consulting (among other industries). You also complete a team project throughout the semester and gives you a great opportunity to work on an operations type project and apply the skills you've learned in class to a real life situation. Professor Bayiz is very nit picky with his comments on homework and presentations, but he means well and is giving you that feedback to ensure you perform well in front of your client and in your future job.

Its a must take class for those planning to pursue career in Ops Consulting. You will learn how to think like a consultant. The professor is a consultant hence he provides templates, frameworks that are used within the industry. He is always available and is very quick with his email responses.

The professor is extremely knowledgeable and was helpful in pointing our group in the right direction for a more specific problem to dive into for our project. The cases are not recent though, so less relevant to today's operational problems. Still helpful for me to learn as someone with no relevant experience.

Dasu is a good professor and very knowledgeable in this field. If you plan on working in healthcare at all the exposure on the projects in this class is really awesome. 

The class can be kind of boring and it being from 630-930 doesn't help but it is very helpful in understanding how and why the healthcare system is the way that it is.

I was most excited for this class this semester and was severely disappointed by the constant repetition of the same lessons in class (basically Dasu just says "hospitals are inefficient, use Lean tactics blah blah blah"). It's a very limited view on Healthcare Operations, only focuses on provider, not inclusive of the lack of incentive alignment across the HC supply chain. Project/consulting work was VERY good, I learn a lot from my client (LA County Emergency Dept), however Dasu kept limited our team's potential to make an impact and was disrupting the relationship with the client, it's been very frustrating.

Dasu is a great professor who really wants students to gain a better understanding of healthcare industry. Not having a final is a nice bonus. However, if project is not very engaging there is a limit to how much some students would enjoy the class.

Excellent operations class and a must for anyone interested in healthcare. Great guest speakers, cool projects to work on with real companies/hospitals. Always over-subscribed so make sure you get in!

The professor should be allowed to make this almost an entirely project based course. I am not receiving much value from the cases/class time but the consulting project has been amazing and a great learning experience.

Excellent class and taught by an excellent professor. 3 taking it even if you are not interested in healthcare - insightful discussions and assignments that have applications across the MBA curriculum board. Diverse class as well - not just MBA students so you get a rounded perspective. 3 taking.

If you are interested in working in healthcare/healthcare consulting (payer/provider) this class is very useful. Mostly a project based course, working with a well known hospital provider solving real world problems. There is a decent amount of reading, half the class is data analysis, while the other half is analyzing cases. Professor Dasu is very knowledgable on the subject as he consults for the companies you would be working with. Can be a bit boring at times.

Very useful class for those interested in operations, even those with no particular interest in healthcare as many of the skills are transferable. Excel and other softwares used for analytics, modeling, etc (class starts with very basic skills which are probably repetitive for many MBAs but also moves into other topics like time series modeling. Project-based class with outside companies where the value of the class depends somewhat on the project you get assigned. Medium/high amount of work mostly focused on consulting project.

Class is pretty dry but the cases are useful and well-selected. The big selling point of this class is the consulting project - extremely valuable in getting some real-world experience if you're looking at healthcare consulting, and the international experiences are amazing if you're looking for that as well. My consulting project for a healthcare company in a foreign country was absolutely one of the highlights of my time at Marshall as an MBA. Do note that you will need to fund your travel yourself if you decide to pursue that option. If you have no interest in healthcare then don't take this, otherwise it's an obvious fit since it's hard to find other coursework looking at healthcare at Marshall.
There are some overlapping contents with Operartions Management
Homework assignments are very long. Be sure to try to get ahead start.
great opportunity to work with innovative clients

The discussions and lectures move SLOW, but the curation of topics is excellent for a survey on health care operations. All of the projects offered looked really good and interesting. It's definitely the most interesting project I'm working on this semester! I'm absolutely sure I'll be applying what I'm learning in my healthcare career. Dasu is a super kind person.

If you are interested in the healthcare industry as a future function highly recommend this class. You explore topics beyond just the operations aspects of healthcare and the projects you get to chose from cover a broad range of applications so you can really dive deep where you are the most curious / passionate. Prof Dasu is not always the most engaging lecturer but is a nice person and very flexible with the project to make sure your team can be successful.

career: Entrepreneurship;Other | Business Development and Strategy within the Biotech, Pharma, and Healthcare sectors
comments:
We work with real-world clients, which can sometimes make scheduling meetings and coordinating timings challenging. The course equally integrates operations and data science. It includes individual homework assignments, quizzes, and group work.
Who is this class for? Students interested in operations in healthcare
Final Thoughts: Overall, working with real-world clients is a valuable experience, though the project can be quite vast, which may limit your ability to contribute significantly. However, it provides a great glimpse into the operations side of the healthcare system. Professor Dasu is an excellent instructor.

career: Consulting;Entrepreneurship | Health Care Consulting and Entrepreneurship
comments:
Who is this class for? If you are interested in working on the provider side of the healthcare industry, then this is a great course that gives us the opportunity to work with real-world clients.
Final Thoughts: Professor Dasu is highly knowledgeable and one of the best instructors I have had so far. He makes the class very engaging by sharing his 20+ years of experience working with clients in the healthcare industry. Professor Cosimo teaches the analytical part of the course, and he is very good at it.

Workload is very manageable, mostly focused on the semester-long group project and studying for quizzes. You rank your preferences for a list of projects at the start of the semester. Best course for those interested in healthcare roles after graduation.

This was a great class, more MBAs should take it. It's pretty much analyzing what operational levers you (as a manager) will be able to affect in order to influence financial measures (namely ROA). This is a great class, the professor is so enthusiastic about the subject matter, Marshall MBAs need to take classes like this. I believe this is where our weaknesses lie (as Marshall), take this 1.5 unit class, especially if Ops isn't your "thing".

Not bad for a 1.5 unit class. Course was a lot heavier on the financial side than expected, but Prof. Zhu was quite helpful and good to work with. It's easy to zone out of class and not pay attention, but he's actually really smart and has a lot of good insights + contacts in many industries. Not a lot of work, but some essays and cases have page length requirements. Final report and presentation is determined by your group, so you can decide on the scope as preferred.

This course was being taught for the first time and was disorganized and unfocused. Didn't meet my expectations for a DSO class, all big-ideas and soft-skills, don't feel I've learned much about data. Aside from final group project, very little work outside of class. Final project is for Sony Pictures, and while it's been useful to talk about in interviews, in practice it hasn't been a beneficial project at all.

comments: This class was very unorganized and not super valuable. It was very repetitive (always talking about a case, pros and cons of the industry, pros and cons of how big data can be used to help the company).
topic_title: DSO 599 Special Topics: Getting the Organization Ready for Big Data

comments: Nice guy -- I feel like this is probably his first time teaching. Weird open-ended class structure. Guest speakers are cool. Project is largely unrelated to anything we do in class.
topic_title: DSO 599 Special Topics: Getting the Organization Ready for Big Data
DSO 599 Special Topics: Getting the Organization Ready for Big Data
DSO 599 - Special Topics: Generative AI and Automation: Business and Societal Implications

comments: This class is pretty hands-on, perhaps too technical for most MBAs. It shows you the applications of AWS for ML and AI - a behind-the-scenes peek into what everyone's talking about. The coding (primarily python, with bits of YAML and JSON thrown in), can be sometimes confusing, especially getting AWS setup in the initial classes. Sign up only if you're prepared to put in the work to reseach and correct your code (Professor provides examples, but often you need to putter around to solve the take home problem), and spend $$ on AWS subscription (it cost me $35 halfway into the semester). After taking this course, you should be able to have the baseline knowledge to engage in decent conversations around machine learning, AI, LLMs and the whole gamut but you will by no means become a technical expert.
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics:  Hands-on Data Analytics and Machine Learning in AWS Cloud

comments: The class content seems to be tempting for someone pursuing the tech industry, but this course requires a high understanding of coding, cloud computing, AI, and ML technology itself rather than a business-wise perspective. The professor encourages helping each other between students, however, the problem is only a few students can help other people (maybe!), and there is no TA.
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics:  Hands-on Data Analytics and Machine Learning in AWS Cloud

comments: The class needs you to have basic coding knowledge to get the most out of it or you will need to spend at least 6-8 hours to keep up. The hands on project work will help you add a talking point to resume. Tldr: needs effort, not an easy class; very useful if you are interested and ready to spend 4 hrs min every week outside class
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics:  Hands-on Data Analytics and Machine Learning in AWS Cloud

comments:
Mix of lectures on the history of tech platforms and class discussion about strategic decisions FAANG giants have made when competing with each other. Professor is intentionally a lenient grader, more interested in provoking interesting debate than having class "learn" anything. Professor is a working professional and I get the sense he does this for fun so class energy is positive and he's genuinely interested in getting to know everyone.
Who is this class for? Great for big picture thinkers who are interested in how the tech business got to be where it's at today and what it might look like in the future.
Final Thoughts: Strange that this is with DSO department as it's really a strategy class. There's NOTHING quantitative about it. Lots of MSBA students when I took it, fun to meet new people but first couple classes feel like a review of strategy classes that MBAs have taken but that aren't required for MSBA.
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics: Battles For Our Digital Ecosystems (Lessons from the Field)

comments: Brand new professor who makes it a point to embarrass students if they have to leave early or arrive late, After the entire class told him that we were not interested in programming, the course was supposed to be about AI topics. He insisted on making us learn advanced programming. This class is for people who know how to code only.
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics: Battles For Our Digital Ecosystems (Lessons from the Field)

comments:
This is a very light course when it comes to course workload, and the professor is a titan of industry. It is a very valuable course if you are hoping to learn more about the way companies compete in the digital space (across Software, Hardware, AI, Infrastructure, Customers).
Be prepared for long discussions, where your attention will definitely be rewarded with some great takeaways about the industry and your career as a whole
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics: Battles For Our Digital Ecosystems (Lessons from the Field)

comments: Class is light on details, structure is guest speakers and cases with a few papers throughout the semester. The class is very dependent on who else is in the room for discussion, but the topics are applicable to any field. This is not a class about AI tools and should not be taken for that reason alone.
topic_title: DSO 599 - Special Topics: Fast & Flow Strategy: Mastering Real-Time Business in AI Age

comments:
1) If you are unfamiliar with investment banking, this class is a great introduction. Walks through each step of a middle-market investment banking deal.
2) Professors are passionate and knowledgeable, but lack academic professionalism in terms of class time management, using cold calls rather than "stop me if I'm going to fast" to assess student learning, and other standards of high-quality education. They created a great course structure that familiarizes students, and they are very available despite their full-time work at their respective investment banks.
3) Industry insight high. Workload expectations average.
Brian is a practitioner. Very engaging and makes the 630 wed nights enjoyable. He also brings in interesting guest speakers.
Who is this class for? One should take this elective if interested in pursuing Investment Banking
Really easy course and covers the basics of sell-side M&A banking process. More like a career exploration course but doesn't go deeper on the different facets of IB since it's only 6 weeks long.

Minimal assignments with pretty easy grading and one midterm that was graded fairly. Ideal class for someone going into investment banking. Making connection with professor (Brian Little) is one of the selling points; he is super approachable and makes lectures interesting with guest speakers and humor spread throughout.
It's a pretty laid back course with a very impressive instructor who's an MD at Lincoln Capital. He brings in interesting guest speakers and the class is graded generously.
Very useful even if you aren’t pursuing investment banking

The topics discussed on class are really updated and they covers the main categories in Fin-tech industry. There will be a speaker for each class, and the teachers are really interesting! Whether you are interested into the new trend of finance, or interested into entrepreneur, you should take this class.

One mid term, one more quiz (packed due to the tight schedule, but very doable), and a final project as of Spring 2024.

comments: Even though this class has a slow start (the first few weeks focus on CAPM and basic equity pricing models), once we get into the "behavioral" and "psychological" part of investing, the class is very engaging. Professor Hirshleifer is a reasonable grader and the curve is adequate.

This is an amazing class. If you are interested in behavioral fallacies and the quantification of those fallacies, this is fantastic. It cuts through the bulllshit that plagues economics classes, which is the assumption that everyone acts perfectly rationally. Light workload (only 3 psets and a final) and so far it's been extremely straightforward. Hopefully Cary can continue teaching this class.

I enjoy this class as the course material is enticing to me, with a good balance of qualitative theories and quantitative practises. The assignments are interesting, with exposure to theorectical debates and trading strategies. The professor is very attentive to our questions, and very approachable despite his prestige and reputations in the field

The class is more theoretical & academic - not as practical as I hoped it was going to be. We will mention something like 'hedge funds take advantage of this,' but I wish we were able to have more quantitative practice with how to analyze stock prices and other metrics and/or hedge/short/etc. against biases. Very nice professor, but often over-complicates things when explaining intuitive ideas.
Who is this class for? Not necessarily for finance people, people interested in more academic/economic theory
Final Thoughts:

This class should be amazing, but the professor drops the ball. The speakers, cases and material are all great, but good luck understanding it all. His lectures consist of 100 slides that can be incoherent at times, if you can learn on your own and have a solid team, then you'll get something out of this class.

comments: This is a good class to take if you have no prior knowledge of venture capital or private equity. Scott moves really fast but you just have to tell him to slow down. Material can be complex and Scott can be all over the place but he's always willing to help.
Scott is great and really cares about his students. He moves quickly and sometimes allows students to derail conversations but for the most part you'll learn a ton in this class

Great professor who is entertaining and cares about his student learning. He moves fast and it will be difficult to stay on top of if you're not quant-minded, but its very useful and he is a patient professor

Abrams is hands down one of the, if not the best professor at Marshall. An absolute joy and brings his experience to discussions as well. Easy to learn actual concepts and helped immensely with finance recruiting

Scott is an amazing professor and really cares about his students. Finance is not my strength but this class is very applicable and I've learned a ton! If you do the practice problems and pay attention in class you will be fine.

Scott is amazing. He zooms through the material, which can be hard to follow if finance isn't your strong suit, but he's super patience if you have questions. Doing the practice problems helps with the  group projects and the quizzes. Take the class for Scott. It's worth it.

Very useful class and Abrams keeps it interesting and engaging (guys, guys, guys!) Must take if you're into finance and very good general knowledge even if not, would say it could be a borderline core requirement. Teaching style could be a bit more organized and easy to follow though.

Abrams is a great professor at making sure everyone understands what's happening in course. He also provides a lot of examples that make it engaging. As somebody not going into finance or without a finance background, outside of Corporate Finance, I've learned a lot from working with classmates regarding the our projects.

This is a really great class and is quite engaging if you put the effort in. The class is rewarding, I have learned a significant amount.

The class is not easy, but Scott is generous about the grades. You can get useful valuation knowledge from this class. A lot of team projects, so, you'd better have other electives less time consuming.

Coming from a pure tech background, I had no idea about Finance in general. Scott constantly ties in the class material to how it is relevant for banking and equity research.
it's a good review of the valuations basics and relates directly with my post-MBA role. It pairs well with the M&A elective.
if I ever participate in an acquisition on either side of the table, I'll be utilizing skills learned in this class.

I never considered myself a finance person, and this has truly been my favorite class I've taken at Marshall.  The material is challenging, but totally doable if you study and come to class. Hard class for those who don't have a finance background, but I'd recommend if you like a challenge and liked corporate finance.

Professor Abrams really cares about his students and wants to see us succeed. Definately a hard class especially if you struggle with Finance classes, but Prof Scott goes  a long way to help you feel confortable with the content. This class demands hard work but it is worth it. Scott is an amazong professor and human being. I would say, forget the grade and do this class for the learning. An MBA must!

I do not come from a finance or business background so one of my goals coming to grad school was to immerse myself in courses outside my comfort zome that would push me to grow. This class fit that bill. Valuations feels like an extension of the core finance course. Scott is one of my favorite professors so far at Marshall and I really appreciate how we will work with each student to meet them at their finance level. I think this class is great for anyone looking to pursue finance or anyone just wanted to learn more about finance and how it fits into the larger business puzzle.

This class is a great Tier 2 finance course. Scott, although moves very quickly, is understanding and helps students conceptualize many of the nuances in a Balance Sheet/Income Statement/Statement of Cash Flows. Additionally, he ties fundamental analysis to overall valuation of a company in a simple manner that is easy to follow. To dinge him slightly, sometimes the numbers utilized for his examples are not correct, which requires correction. However, without a finance background, these errors can lead to significant confusion. Overall, however, Scott is a rockstar.

Scott is an amazing professor He moves through the content quickly but you will mot be left behind if you do the work and go to office hours. I chose this class because I enjoyed Scott's teaching style in the core finance course and I was looking to broaden my knowledge despite finance not being my future intended field. I do think this class is a great way to dive deeper into how finance fits into buisnesses overall in a practical and enjoyable way. Cases are interesting.

Scott is a fantastic professor who cares deeply about helping his students understand the concepts of valuation.  While Scott is certainly a fast mover and quick talker, this makes his classes rarely boring and ever dynamic.  His use of references to his career help to illuminate the course and provide a unique persepective.

Extension of corporate finance class. Scott is incredibly engaging, structures the class in an organized way, and brings in real world experience as well as case and hands-on practice to supplement the theory and make the content come alive. Highly recommend even if you are not going into finance. If you attend class, pay attention, do the homework (mostly group work) and additional practice problems, and don't just try to do the bare minimum, you will do just fine in this class, even if you are not going into banking.

The class offers little emphasis on "Valuation". Yes, you will learn to do DCF and Comps, however, in my opinion offers little insights into nuances of valuation and actually going about securities analysis to have any practical relevance.

As others have mentioned, Scott does move quickly, which can be challenging for those without finance backgrounds. However, all the material is in the lectures, so if you go back and rewatch them, you'll probably pick up everything you need to know.
Practical skills for financial valuation so if you want to learn how to get into that job function take this class. Abrams goes fast though so be sure to give him your full attention.

As the other comments seem to suggest, the experiences with Professor Abrams and Professor Ku are different, and I prefer the latter. Ku is probably trying to match her desire for the class to see beyond the newsprint and formulae with a need to bring everyone along with the rigour of the class. The concepts covered are not very many, and except for LBO, everything is covered in the core Corp Fin class. Valuations is considered a must-have MBA elective, because I think it is supposed to teach you how to value anything in terms of money (or more specifically in time value of money). Ku does an excellent job with this concept. For example "dividend is the liquidation of equity", "DCF is the most convincing because YOU have done the math, most likely with just an Excel sheet." The assignments can become needlessly complex, so check with her about expectations. Mid terms are hard, but not hard for hard's sake. Guest lectures are great, and Prof Ku is very motivational as a person.

Ku clearly loves her subject and loves talking about it, which is good. Her lectures contain frequent digressions and long periods with no actual hard content covered, which is not good. Not nearly enough time is spent instructing and offering practice in actual calculations; too much theory and concepts, not enough practical application. And assignment directions are often vague and/or unclear.

Dean Ku has such great intentions in teaching this course but as someone who is not skilled in finance, I've really struggled to understand her teaching style and lectures. She often assumes students know much more about finance than they really do and believes students can intuit answers rather than learn them. Because of this, her descriptions of concepts are often vague and unclear and I've resorted to finding outside support in this class to make up for the gap. Valuations is an important topic to learn but know that you'll likely be teaching yourself a lot of this course if you decide to take it and do not have a finance background.

Challenging class with a lot of content, which is all extremely helpful if your future job function involves anything to do with valuations or analyzing financial statements. Scott Abrams speaks fast so it is important to pay attention in class. The workload is manageable, but does require some effort.

Lecture was lacking for this class, some good guest speakers were here, but the professor wasn't really interested in teaching, provided minimum lecture and often wandered off the topic. She was very knowledgeable but you have to

Really slow pace. 10 weeks in we're still reviewing stuff from core finance

Case heavy, discussion-based, and Professor gives lectures free-style. Professor Ku is not for everyone, she's the complete opposite of Scott Abrams. Fun class if you like discussions, cases, and plan to join SIF
Feel like everything i learned in this class is covered by corp finance

Best professor. Makes material easier to understand. Valuations is a good skill to have in general, but the class may be entirely different an potentially more difficult if not for Scott.
Great class taught by a great professor. the class goes through key valuation topics in depth.

Take this class if you are going into consulting. Super useful (and I wish I had taken it before my summer internship). Scott moves fast, but you can rewatch the videos. Definitely a lot to learn and takeaway

Have a good understanding of corp fin before joining. Scott is a great professor and makes the material easy to understand but he moves quickly. The material is also very connected to real world situations so it helps in more than actually evaluating companies

Weekly quizzes on the readings where the class isn't taught how to do the calculations until after the quizzes. Also, 70% of the grade is on the final. Class is too advanced unless you have an extensive M&A finance background.

Professor Weinstein is a complete ASS. He assigns quizzes every week which contain heavy financial analysis that the class does not teach you how to solve. This professor honestly just doesn't give a damn about teaching students and its evident in his demeanor. Worst class i've ever taken in my life - honestly i should be reimbursed my tuition for this class.
It's a solid cased-based class that teaches strategy through a financial lens. If you are going into consulting, the analyses performed may be useful to your work.

Griffiths expects everyone in the class to have a thorough and complete financial understanding, without him teaching us most of the content. Course content is interesting, but the organization of the course needs a lot of work.

**By the time you read this, Prof Weinstein will have retired**
 1) Best non-core class I have taken. Best non-core professor by far.

 3) Warning: This class is hard. If you didn't do well in Core Corporate Finance (A), brush up or take valuation before starting this class. 70% of course grade is the final exam, which is a 5-hour take-home modeling-heavy case assignment.

The class is enjoyable and the case-based nature of it puts what you are learning into context. I feel like I am getting information that will be helpful in a role within corporate finance and eventually as CFO. I still find the class enjoyable and interesting and I really like Professor Griffith's style and general demeanor.

"This is a class where you end up getting whatever you put into it. He gives lectures for the first 4 weeks, and then the class become almost entirely case-based. Subject can be difficult, but I learned a lot. Midterm, Final, few hws, group project. Reasonable amount of work. Did a great job of teaching the basics. Got somewhat difficult at the end though because he tried to cram a lot of complicated material into a few classes.

Interesting course topic on how Hedge Funds work/function, however the material is repeated many times over - even guest lecturers will present on most of the same topic. This class is an easy A, but should really be a one-off, three hour seminar. Not nearly enough new information here to warrant the $ you will spend.

This class is basically a speaker series + a series of basic hedge fund strategies and fundamental verbiage/understanding you must have to get into the industry. Mick does a great job but the class is not going to change your life. It's a fairly basic class designed for basic understanding of the world of hedge funds. That being said, the speakers are incredible and interesting.

The speakers are fantastic and are the real value add of this course. The class is extremely unstructured so beware of that when registering for the course. Structrue is atypical of a Marshall course, but useful for those seeking careers in Investment Managment / the Hedge Fund industry.
Very high-quality class. Very chill and knowledgable professor. Plus very high-quality guest speaker sessions.

This class is really practical and helpful if you want a good handle on financial modeling, whether or not you want to pursue banking (I am though). And there's really not a lot of homework and never any pre-work.

I would not recommend this professor at all. He spends way too much time going over simple, straightforward aspects of Excel. He also spends too much time explaining what he's going to teach on a given day and not enough time actually teaching that topic. I'm not sure how this class would be with a different professor, I'm sure a bit better cause it'd be tough to make it worse than it currently is.

This class is what you make of it... sounds very vague, but 100% true. The solutions for the homework assignments are already given so you can basically copy/paste answers. However, if you go through and rebuild the models he has taught, you gain extensive modeling knowledge. Additionally, his lectures are very engaging. He dives into interesting financial concepts then ties the concepts to the models so you get academic and practical knowledge. Additionally, he is hilarious with his stories... makes the learning environment that much more engaging.

A very unique class, which is extremely exercise based.  The course is useful for those targeting a P/E / Investment Banking career.  It is not quite what I thought it would be when signing up for the course, in the sense that it is not the type of course to teach you spreadsheet tips and tricks necessarily, although these are sprinkled in.  The course truly does aim to provide you the IB internship experience, so if that is what you want, the course is a must take.

This is a class for IB or P/E, as stated above. As you might imagine from the name (though I didn't sufficiently get this before enrolling) it is very heavy on the finance concepts and details. Less about the excel modeling of it, though those tricks are shared somewhat. My main criticism is that for those who have less experience in finance, it can go quite quickly as he'll pick up on the understanding of the IB kids in the class and think that they speak for everyone. He also will lecture about what we're going to do, without actually showing it in action, and then we go and do it, whereas a more helpful structure might to be to lecture as he's doing it. All this being said, if you're going into a finance-heavy workplace and really do concentrate and work at the material, I imagine it would be helpful.

Professor cares about students but his concept of what an IB associate/analyst does day to day is outdated. Training the Street gives more real world application for modeling. Many concepts taught in this class will never be used on the desk

The professor is very engaging in lectures and shows care for students. I would agree with my peers that a lot of this class is what you make of it from a homework perspective. This class could be a nice stepping stone for some exposure to basic excel modeling, but nothing surpasses on-the-job training in this stuff from what I can tell.

His course could be valuable to someone that seeks a career in investment management.

Struggled to find applicability of the class.

Final Thoughts: Professor sits up front, lectures the whole time, with 0 slides. He lectures from a textbook that he wrote. 

8 random in person quizzes so you need to show up to every lecture, even though they are monotonous and fairly boring.

comments: Really interesting class and valuable. Fields is funny and entertaining, although sometimes based on the content the class can be dry, but it's a good class and you learn a lot. Be prepared for a lot of reading though!

Nice non-quant class that balanced out my quant-heavy schedule. Interesting stories and concepts, especially on contracts. Class is all lecture, and not too heavy in terms of workload. Not an essential course, but relatively fun and interesting.
Great professor and a lot of practical knowledge given in lectures.
Great professor. It is an easy class to pass, but you actually learn really useful information about the US legal system. I highly 3 it.
Course can get stuck in the weeds and minutiae some times, but Fields is hysterical, and covers an important knowledge area that no other courses at Marshall touch

A useful overview of the law and how it relates to the most common business applications (hiring, product liability, etc). Very useful particularly for people thinking about running/owning their own business. Fields is hysterical and keeps dense subject matter light and understandable.

At this point in time, I don't have a strong sense that I will use much of this content, but I do think there are some lectures that will be valuable at some point in my career. Fields is a very entertaining professor, and I love the 80 minutes in his class because of his teaching style. I learn a lot about the law while doing the 5 question quizzes, and have struggled through the two midterms (like many of my peers). To do well in this class, it would require a good amount of reading and studying outside of class lectures.

This can be a useful class but its not a must. Exams are tough but course overall is not too complicated. The professor is quite hilarious and enjoyable and imparts a lot of personal experience from his law practice. Can be a good offset if you have other tough classes.

In corporate strategy, having even a baseline understanding of business law concepts will be so helpful in the planning and deal-making I anticipate in the future. Fields is both knowledgeable and personable. The concepts can feel difficult to grasp all at once, but if you actually read the textbook (really not hard unless you cram it into 24 hours before a midterm) you will pick up more than you expect!
Decent course, but Fields is hilarious and makes it worthwhile.

This is one of the best and most useful classes I have taken at Marshall. Most of us will likely be dealing with contracts and other aspects of the law at various points throughout our business careers, and thanks to this class I will be much better prepared to do so. Fields comes off as dry at first but don't let that scare you away; he's extremely sharp, laid-back, and also hilarious! Tests are fair and the workload is completely reasonable; you just need to keep up with the reading and do one group project, which actually turned out to be really interesting. Take this class. You won't regret it.

If there is one class that will provide you a whole toolbox of what to do when it comes to business law, this is it. Super important topics are taught around contracts, litigation, intellectual property, torts, etc. You will need this information in business and life for sure! The professor is kinda old and not always PC, but he is a crazy skilled lawyers with great stories about real business law cases he has worked (and won!) and I feel like I've learned a lot. Also an easy A.

Very useful content, especially if you want to be a business owner or leader in any company. Agree with everything in the synopsis from the line above. If you've ever been interested in learning about law this is the perfect amount of work/info to get a great foundation without having to put in too much work. Honestly, the content in this class has been one of the the most useful/interesting of all my Marshall classes.
Fields takes a very dry topic and makes it engaging by peppering in his own relevant anecdotes. It's a pleasure to be in the class.

Interesting class with a kind and nice professor, workload is light, and if you actually pay attention and go to class (not required at all) you will have a good time and learn some interesting things related to law and business. Not necessarily an easy A but a very easy pass and if you try a good grade should be obtained
Very dry lecture style, sometimes has a funny and relevant story sprinkled in, but it's a lot of nitty gritty legal technicalities.

The class covers key business-related legal topics at a fairly high level. Not enough of course that you won't need a lawyer, but hopefully enough to keep you from doing something stupid in a contract negotiation, or getting sued. Good class, Fields is a fun guy.

Very, very useful class that gives you a broad overview of the most important legal concepts that a business student should know. I honestly think this could even be a core class. Workload so far is moderate, class is also of medium difficulty (neither super hard, nor super easy). The professor is a funny guy, he likes ot tell stories which makes the class entertaining but I sometimes wish he would stick a little more to the script. Nonetheless, it's a good class and I recommend it.
Helpful for anyone who will one day be a business leader. Fields is a great professor and very entertaining as well.

Good class overall. Fields makes it fun, and aims to give students a good base knowledge of business law. He is also absolutely hilarious and I think half the reason he teaches is just to tell jokes every day.

Love this class.  Challenging quizzes and exams, but very easy class sessions.  Straight lecture, no cold calling, lots of humor.  Fields takes a dry subject matter and makes it interesting with personal anecdotes and examples.  Also no class participation grade which is cool.

Fields has forgotten more law than you or I will ever know. He has great stories. That said, Fields does NOT do a good job of setting expectations with respect to projects, assignments, or tests, so you sometimes feel like you are just throwing stuff against the wall to see what sticks. His quiz/test questions are also worded confusingly (that's the lawyer in him); he sometimes has a hard time translating law-speak into plain English. This can be very frustrating. Come to learn, just don't care about your grade because you have a limited amount of control over it.
Fields is an engaging professor. His annecdotes are always interesting and entertaining. As the person above mentioned, quizzes and exams can be hard. Long live the curve.

Easy class but very informative and useful.
Who is this class for? A student who is interested in law and wants to connect with a great professor.

Fields is an interesting cat. He definitely knows his shit, but he is also very rough around the edges. Academically, it's a pretty straightforward class. Take home quizzes, three exams, and no real projects. If anything take it for Field's random anecdotes about his experiences in the law field.

comments: If I was to answer the question: "Which one class do you want to add as a recommended Elective for all MBA?", it will be this one. The class is very practically grounded - employment, liability, contracts, torts, employer relations, etc. Some of this is probably not going to kick in until later in our careers, but this is all insanely practical. Everything else about the professor holds - hard quizzes, great stories, confusing wording. The thing about quizzes: while the wording is hard, once you know how he sets the options, it is hard. There is only one option that is answerable based on his book. Oh, and by the way, the book is kindda $$, but you need it. He is also quite reachable as long as you email him about 10-12 hours prior. Overall, it is one of the classes that gives you an entirely new viewpoint to look at the world, just enough to process legal stuff and be mindful of a need to get counsel. Does not take roll.

If you are incredibly into the theory behind finance this might be the course for you, but for most I think it is quite abstract and dry.
This class can be dry but the information is useful if you care about finance/tax/M&A. Straight ppt lectures every day but he is super knowledgeable and a nice guy.

Extremely helpful during office hours. His class goes at a decent pace.
Best elective this semester and best course I've had all year.

"NOTE: I am NOT a Finance/banking person and I still love this class.

One of the best classes I've taken at Marshall. While it can get a bit quantitative or technical at times, the class is run really well. Not too much work, but very real-world applicable information.

Great finance overview that delves into topics learned in Core. Professor Hoberg also brings the class to life with a true joy in students understanding concepts.
Exactly as advertised. Professor Hoiberg is a bit dry but extremely knowledgeable on the topic and academically challenging for students of all levels of experience in M&A.

Great content and probably ranks near the top in understanding business valuations. Material is really interesting but class is hard. Lots of case studies. Hoberg can be a bit monotone, but his content and knowledge is really great.

Hoberg has the most boring voice ever, but he records his classes so you don't have to physically be there. You should have some basic understanding of finance before taking this class (beyond corp fin a+b). I have zero experience/knowledge in finance, and it is way above my capability to actually learn anything in here.

Just take this class, it's great.  excellent even

This class exceeded my expectations. I'm not the strongest in finance, but my intended strategy work will heavily incorporate M&A analysis. Hoberg explains concepts much better than my professors did during core, plus with an adorable enthusiasm that's chuckleworthy throughout. The readings are a bit dry, but the online discussions add a lot. I feel like I now have a better understanding of some quantitative skills I needed during core, but even better is my new approach to qualitative understanding of synergies between companies.

Jerry is an expert and can talk about this stuff forever. He does have quite the monotone voice though and some cheesy jokes. This class can get pretty technical so if you did well in core finance, you should be fine here. Definitely challenging but a great class to take if you are generally interested in M&A
Hoberg is truly an expert in his field and one of the best profs I've had at USC. Hits all areas of M&A and is very lecture heavy (which I prefer over discussion).

I chose to take this class to strengthen my technical understanding of M&A. Professor Hoberg is very thorough, knowledgeable and patient. I would recommend taking Valuations before enrolling in this class if you do not have a solid finance background.

Builds on Corporate Finance with an initial focus on technical valuation methodologies (CAPM, DCFs, etc.) and then focuses on more broad lessons (what types of mergers traditionally generate the most value etc.). He has a very dry voice, which can make lectures a bit boring, but ultimately the content is good and I'd recommend to anyone in finance, especially anyone doing sell-side M&A work or corporate development.
Class is focused far more on strategy than anything math/modeling related. His lectures surrounding strategy are interesting and engaging, but he's not as good at explaining the quantative portions.
Midterm, Final, two group cases, and participation

Professor Hoberg is very passionate about the course and it is clear he wants his students to learn and do well. A finance background is not necessary to do well in the class either. I enjoy attending class sessions and have learned a lot, which I can hopefully use as I begin a career in consulting.

This class is a must for aspiring Investment Bankers. Professor Hoberg is great professor with exceptional depth of understanding of the relevant concepts and practical nuances. The course is really engaging both inside and outside the class. The dealchat forum on blackboard ensures the learning continues outside the class and draw upon exceptional insights from peers taking the class. The dry sense of humor and Professor's wit will ensure you enjoy the class thoroughly.

Hoberg is a gem. This is a really interesting class, and Hoberg does a great job taking what can be dense or complex subject matter and making it accessible. He provides plenty of opportunities for participation both in class and on the blackboard discussion board. Such a good experience, highly recommend Hoberg.

The class material and cases are very interesting. The professor is very knowledgeable and happy to help students explore questions. I have found it particularly interesting to take the previous finance knowledge I had and stretch it to scenarios I haven't worked on in previous jobs. Would be very helpful to pick case teams using strategy of incorporating at least 1-2 people who have prior modeling experience. Great list of guestspeakers (strategic, PE, search funds, IB, private credit) that gives you a holistic view of the M&A world. Perhaps not as technical and lecture-focus as the other professor's M&A class, but you still need to read cases every week for assignment purposes.

The way that Professor Hoberg teaches could be dry, but the quality of the class is definitely very high. One of the very few high-quality classes in Marshall. If you are interested in M&A, don't miss it! I suggest to take the Financial Analysis and Valuation class before taking M&A. M&A class is buit on that class and is not easy.
Structured class and very nice Professor, covering pretty much all the critical concepts related to M&A.

Professor Hoberg is actually one of the best and most polished professors at Marshall. At times I wish he was teaching another (more useful) subject aside from Mergers & Acquisitions. I will be referencing this class many, many years into the future in my career, and Prof. Hoburg is one of my favorite professors at Marshall. I recommend everyone take this class.
