comments: This course is essential to the MBA program and to becoming a future leader ready to lead diverse teams regardless of industry designation. This subject matter is tough to discuss and pushes people outside their comfort zone. It is an excellent opportunity to educate students and professionals about the value of diverse individuals, perspectives and livelihoods. This course addresses and provides instruction regarding the types of equity, diversity, and inclusion in detail. Each topic discussed has key takeaways and well developed presentations to go along with lecture. As a topic, EDI can be uncomfortable especially for people who are ignorant regarding the topic. However, this is positive and reflective of the changing nature of many businesses developing and succeeding today. Dr. Harper is absolutely the best professor that USC has to teach this course. He encourages all students to speak out and provide their thoughts to learn more about working together. and leading diverse teams. Dr. Harper employs the use of videos, lectures, cases, group work, in class exercises and guest speakers to teach material. He also pushes people outside of their comfort zone to work in teams that are not homogenous. This is the first class at USC where people who are diverse can feel safe sharing perspectives without fragile individuals downplaying the value of their voice and intelligence. The workload is very light. The class sessions could be dividied up better some weeks as discussions can run long. There is also room for more breaks to be integrated. The initial weeks were intense and full of content, so there could be a better transition between the first 4-5 weeks and the case group work.
topic_title: MOR 534 - Equity, Diversity and Inclusion in Business

comments: The material that was presented in the first few weeks is incredibly important and I found that to be useful. However, teaching and introducing heavy topics and discussion over the course of a single class period feels rushed. The topics covered are rarely if ever talked about in any of our other classes and are critical for future leaders in business. However, I feel like the execution of the "hands-on" portion of the class makes little sense and can be improved upon. We have not spent minimal class time talking about best practices, which makes the "hands-on" piece feel like we're making things up as we go. Much of the learning is from other classmates' ideas and perspectives, and I think it would be valuable to encourage sharing and structure it more productively. I think that Dr. Harper is able to create a space where marginalized folks feel comfortable sharing their experiences and opinions, but my peers who are not from marginalized groups seem less likely to participate. I am overall glad I took this class, it's the most valuable class I've taken at Marshall thus far, but I do think there is room for improvement.

comments: This is an extremely difficult course subject to teach, but one that is necessary for MBAs as future business leaders. He does often talk about his accomplishments, but so does every other Marshall professor. In regards to some students who feel as though there aren’t key takeaways that are outlined at the end of the class, I want to offer a different perspective. The cases we discuss aren’t like normal case studies that have been edited for educational content, and that come with a lecture and a summary of key concepts. These are real world issues that are complex and can’t be summarized into a few bullet points. Dr. Harper messages that the class is a safe space, but some classmates no longer feel comfortable speaking. While it is important that the class be an environment in which everyone’s opinions are valid, I will say these conversations are supposed to make people feel uncomfortable. It's an interesting class. The cases are good. You learn some good stuff about organizational structure and some life hacks that the professor loves to share

Ken is a wonderful professor and he brings interesting and diverse guest speakers to the class. There is a significant amount of group work required for the class, so be prepared to work closely with your assigned team. There is not much time spent in class reviewing the reading, but that doesn't matter much since both the midterm and final are done at home and open note.

Definitely take if you're going into HR/human capital; strongly consider even if you're not. There's a lot of organizational theory that will add another dimension to how you think about corporate strategy, so consider pairing this with a strategy class of some kind. Perlman is a distinct flavor, so you should be able to tell within the first session if it's a good fit or not.. He's very caring and accommodating, grades super thoroughly with tons of feedback, and brings in (mostly) good guest speakers.

This is my favorite class that I have taken so far. Lots of reading and group work, but Perlman himself has a very strong grasp of the material, and has created a positive in-class environment. Really good guest speakers; the tests/case submissions are difficult but fair.

Heavy workload with a lot of projects and readings but very worthwhile 
Who is this class for? Someone focused on managerial positions, future CEOs or other C suite managers 
Final Thoughts:

Some elements of this class is super interesting and I enjoy learning about creating high-performing teams. Perlman cares a lot about his students and it shows in his teaching. This class has a ton of students in other programs and you are assigned groups, so scheduling team meetings can be more difficult since most of the students work full-time.

You can tell the professor is passionate about his topic. However, sometimes the class itself misses the mark and is not engaging. The majority of assignments are team case analyses and he is a harsh grader, but he means well and wants you to continuously learn and improve. Overall, we are learning some important concepts about how to craft effective organizations.

One of the very few high-quality fluffy classes in Marshall. I really like the way how the professor created groups for group assignment. He would ask students to take a simple personality test before creating groups for students. You would find the best group assignment experience ever!

Course examines the many ways that the structure of an organization can help (or hinder) success. Prof Perlman consults in this field professionally so he's highly knowledgeable and engaged. Great class for future COOs or anyone who aspires to upper management. High workload: each class has reading plus 3 team presentations and an exam. If you put a lot into this one you will get a lot out of it.
Your grade depends on your project team. Fill out the survey honestly at the beginning of class. Projects are graded hard

Professor Perlman is a no-BS kind of guy and can seem a bit intimidating but he is very knowledgeable and very kind. I think he tends to talk a lot, but he makes it interesting. He emphasizes leadership, team culture, and organizational structure concepts and that's reflected in the content. It's a 3-hour class once a week, which can be a long time, but you get used to it quick. Assignments are group-based and case-based. I think the most interesting part of this class is the guest speakers he invites. He knows a lot of really cool and accomplished people (leaders in business, the military, non-profits, etc), so I found a lot of value learning from those speakers. I would suggest taking it if you want a class to balance out another more rigorous, quant-heavy course that you're taking.
Grading bit strict, lots of guest speakers (some are irrelevant?) and theories. Some interesting topics.
Very bright and smart professor. Compassionate and knows his stuff well. He is very fair and the workload isn't too much. Mainly revolving group presentations and online exam.

Do you want to hear an old man boast about how amazing he used to be in the consulting profession? Are you excited by rambling, irrelevant stores that drone on for the entire class period and don't address any of the readings you've been assigned? Then this is the professor for you! Seriously - I strongly recommend that you not take classes with Mische.

Old guy talking about his heydays. Boasts a lot about what he has achieved which is distracting at times - Some hyperbole as well, so take it with a pinch of salt. The readings are very good and give insight into the whole consulting industry. He isn't strict about attendance or no electronics policy. Exams are MCQ which helps. Light workload. Took it as it was during internship recruiting season and can miss a few classes to prepare for interviews.

The entirety of this class is the professor talking about consulting. There is no need to show up to class or do the readings, however showing up to class and listening to the professor is actually quite beneficial, and especially good for MBAs looking to go into consulting.

If you need a sleeper class, take this one. He doesn't value class participation as part of your grade so you can not show up, do the readings, and still get an okay grade. 
 I am going into consulting and do not think any of the information he goes over is actually worthwhile. Sigh.

The structure of this class is a little too loose. I like Mische, and he has a lifetime of knowledge, but the class is lacking in terms of actionable content. More focused on ethics and client relationships than anything you'll be doing as a post-MBA consultant.

If you're looking for a CHILL class with not much work => that's a winner.
 
 In terms of level of consulting skills you'll learn?
 Probably close to zero
 
 It is more an introduction to Consulting. What is Consulting? 
 Providing a service to a client and be paid for it. Ok said in one sentence. Now chill for the rest of the semester :D

This class was a complete waste of time. He never discussed the readings in class. The professor is poorly-organized and appears incapable of following the syllabus. This is a complete waste of tuition and I have learned nothing.

Prof. Mische uses the whole class to talk about his stories, he uses the same concepts and frameworks every class. Tests are easy and the group project is poorly designed, we keep doing status reports instead of valuable work.

Mische (as he refers to himself) is actually a really nice guy. He has a tendancy to be all over the place and just tell stories about his past career. Guy is an absolute legend but you don't really learn too much in this class. Mische will have many moments when you're like how was this dude a partner at KPMG and then 5 minutes later he'll do something that makes you understand why he was. The guy is a little bit crazy but if you want a chill class where you don't really have to do much this is the class for you. Just be flexible because Mische will change things all the time but it's usually for the better. If you just suck up to him and stroke his ego, it's an easy A.

This is a class where you'll sit down and listen to the professor talk about his glory days for a couple hours a week. Class was super unorganized (syllabus was 3+ weeks late and we didn't even follow it) and he was super unorganized (class just covered anything he wanted to talk about that day). Probably the worst class I've ever taken.

I didn't learn a lot from this class. Useful for those who wants to learn basic things about the consulting industry (structure, pay, etc) but everything you learn here could probably be learned through a google search. Overall, a super fluff class that has little engagement from most students.

Not a super structured class, more of a networking hour. There are kernels of useful info, but it's a lot of consulting industry background. Also lots of HBS readings...most expensive coursepack I've every purchased at nearly $200!

Professor is nice and wants students to do well.  He will share stories from his past experience in consulting and from his current work.  Feels less academic and more real world which is a good change of pace.  Not too much work.
This class is very much a forum for Mische to share anecdotes from his career as a consultant. Discussions can be interesting but don't expect to learn a ton in this course.
Typical Mische class. You will not learn anything from him. You can learn concepts from the articles he will share.

Open book Quiz, Open book Midterm, Final + few group projects. Required course for the Strategy/Consulting certificate. Put Yes/No ratings because if you actually want to learn and be proud of taking a course, this is not it if it's with Mische. If you want a relatively low effort class, with some last minute cramming, then take this with Mische. He's such an interesting guy in good/bad ways, but entertaining to say the least.

90% of the class sessions are the professor fondly discussing his consulting experience as a partner (he has some interesting stories) and the remaining 10% is time spent discussing the cases that everyone skimmed through 5 minutes before class started. Only take this class with friends who are also recruiting for consulting because it makes it a bit more enjoyable.

Be warned--this class is a super easy B+, very hard A. He only gives out a handful of As meaning you truly can't miss more than a couple questions on exams. The class is literally only useful if you want to be a consultant. Do not take this class thinking "Oh, maybe I'll get some exposure that will help me in some other way." It won't. Mische can be entertaining and will try to sell you hard on the value of his course, but there's a difference between entertaining and actually useful.

Feels like a pointless filler class. Mische's teaching style is a mix of bravado, intimidation, and a glass-house construction of anecdotes disguised as analysis. Some of the reading is interesting, but rarely do we spend time in class digging into those points; instead, we hear fable-like stories from his consulting years which tangentially touch on the topics assigned. We spent an 80-minute class on the definition of "critical reasoning;" overall, not recommended.
Great course.
The prof. knows a lot about Ai and technology but sometimes struggles to explain concepts. Having sid that, if you pay enough attention, there will lots of takeaways and aha moments in the class.
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments:
I will summarize the best and the worst parts. The worst part is the professor trying too hard to convince people that the course is not technical and has a lot of value. I think she needs to do that in the first lecture and be done with that but it gets annoying when she keeps on wasting time justifying the value of the course instead of actually teaching. She also has a habit of not using the whiteboard despite requesting the same. 
Now the best part! This course is a out of a very few courses where with time the value of what you learn builds exponentially! But you need to participate in discussions. If you are active in the class and are trying to evaluate things with an open mind, there would be a lot of "aha!" moments. I definitely  recommend this course
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments: Professor is knowledgeable, but is not quite engaging. But it's lightweight. Good to learn a thing or two about tech strategy with no exams to balance out the heavier courses.
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments: The professor is very passionate about the subject apart from that the course is pretty dry. I am stil trying to figure out the takeaways of this course. Its a little workload course with lot of guest speakers and student lead discussions. However, I still wouldnt suggest taking this course unless you really want to take a course on AI
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments: Really interesting course with extremely relevant topics and she brings in awesome guest speakers. Pretty chill course overall, minimal workload!
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments: Minimal workload. Professor goes over the frameworks over how to think about AI technology. While this is a very, very useful way of thinking about the future of AI, I wish the content was more tangible with more/better real-life cases.
topic_title: MOR 558 - Technology Strategy in the Age of AI

comments: This is a great qualitative course. It is very heavy on case studies, but you dont have to read them in order to get by in the class. You should, however, because they are interesting and Mische has a strong foundation in the subject matter. He can also be a resource for those recruiting for consulting, specifically financial services consulting at KPMG

Content is average. Mische is really generous with his time and advice. The class is really ad hoc and has the tendency to wander. You can get a lot or very little out of the class. 
Great class if you're doing fall recruiting as Mische may be able to give you guidance and is very understanding of consulting recruiting.
Basically story time with the professor. We watch movies every other class period.
Great professor, great class. If you really push yourself to think about the class content and apply it to your personal/professional life, this is an extremely valuable class
t
Voigt goes on a tangent every class - he is interesting and the topic of learning scenario analysis can be very useful, but could be taught better
topic_title: MOR 562 - Strategic Choice and Valuation Analysis

comments: This class was a struggle, especially at 6:30-9:30. I had heard so much about Voigt, and I think I had mistakenly thought that what I was hearing was positive. However, I found him very scattered and hard to follow. The tests and assignments are not only riddled with grammatical and spelling errors, they are also just really difficult to understand. He does not set you up for success; rather, he wants you to "try to figure it out" and then proceeds to make a lot of unprompted and really unexplained assumptions when he solves the problem. I see the value of the content, this is just not the class to learn it.
topic_title: MOR 562 - Strategic Choice and Valuation Analysis

comments: This is honestly one of the best courses I've taken at USC. It is so much work but I've learned so much. I cannot speak highly enough about this class. Every consulting and strategy candidate should take it.
topic_title: MOR 562 - Strategic Choice and Valuation Analysis

comments:
Voigt assigns an unreasonable amount of work. Proceed with extreme caution. Would say the amount of required work in this class equates to a 5 credit class. Also insists that everyone stays unmuted to faciliate more class interaction...only result is more background noise.
[useful field] This class forced me to learn how to a build a mediocre financial model, which I appreciate, however, some of the topics covered in this class feel VERY niche or more relevant for finance people. He loves calling the class "Advanced Strategy" but it sometimes feels like Special Topics in Finance.
topic_title: MOR 562 - Strategic Choice and Valuation Analysis

comments: Worst class ever. Professor is very unorganised. course is not structured and highly not recomended for full time mba students. He caters only to the needs of part time students. Lots and Lots of work to do for every class. He doesnt teach anything but expects you to know everything somehow and finish all assigments. The only thing he talks about in class is his stories and nothing related to course material. You can take this course if you want to suffer for the entire semester.
topic_title: MOR 562 - Strategic Choice and Valuation Analysis
MOR 563 - Advanced Strategy: Competing in Dynamic Environments

comments: Fiss is the absolute man. He is one of the best at leading case discussions, and it is always  fun being in class with him. Read before class so you're ready. But one of the best profs at Marshall!
topic_title: MOR 563 - Advanced Strategy: Competing in Dynamic Environments

comments:
I loved the design thinking aspect of this class. However, the teacher doesn't seem to understand that Master's students are fundamentally different than undergraduate students, and therefore have multiple responsiilities at once. When told I would be skipping to class to attend a networking event it was meant with a lot of attitude and resistance. 

There is also a ton of cases, it is hard to spend 3 hours talking about cases. The design thinking module was great because it was very engaging (but interestingly enough, she was not the one teaching that class).
Good variety of topics. Learned about design thinking, how to think about new business models, industry disruption. She brought in speakers to talk about some of the topics

Lots on content on design thinking, which is the new big thing in business now, apparently. Course load is not heavy but procrastination will set you far back; join a good team or you're screwed. Guest speakers are a tad boring, but class and case discussions are fairly interesting. She's brilliant. Really insightful.

Great new class. Professor Rindova is very passionate about the subject matter focused on industry disruption and design thinking. My only complaint would be the evening classes can get a little long as some classes are just two case discussions which get old in the 3 hr sessions. Still strong recommend, overall really enjoyed the course!
Rindova is clearly knowledgeable in industry, but not an effective teacher. She doesn't know how to lead a case discussion and sucks at responding to questions in class. Pretty useless.

I took this course as one of the electives for the Tech Commercialization certificate and I didn't want to take anymore entrepreneurship classes. Some of the content in this course overlaps other courses that had Design Thinking and Business Model Canvas, so it felt like some stuff wasn't new to me. What is different though is that the professor delivers it slightly different from other courses, but all in all, similar to many other strategy classes where it's case reading and discussion. There is some more interactivity in this class through in class activities/workshops to make it less dry and boring.
Class discussions are disorganized and do not seem well prepared. However, the coursework is not too challenging.

Great content, it's a hot topic right now (human centered design). However, the teacher had a bit of trouble controlling the class at times and making the content riveting. Great design workshop mid semester though.

Design Thinking workshop was superb. Prof is accomplished but is set in stone in her ways and repeats concepts after a while to the point it gets annoying at times. A bit too theoretical and framework oriented. Class discussions are engaging. Need to read cases before every class. Cases are interesting though. So it is a bit heavy workload.

This is a great course if you are interested in the emerging trend around design thinking. Professor Rindova is really passionate about this space and organizes discussions around some interesting content. 
 
 This is a 3 hour class, once a week, with a lot of reading - so be prepared for that. But certainly worth taking.

Professor is a leader in design thinking. Class lectures can be a bit disjointed, but resources give more concrete strategic and innovation frameworks than the core strategy class. Useful for entrepreneurs or anyone wanting to learn design thinking or how to identify and join new markets.

The cases are very interesting and I have been able to speak about the class projects in interviews and they are very relevant to what is happening in business today. Rindova is a fantastic professor and I have learned a lot in this class. I would definitely recommend this course.

It's a great first elective class, as it will address a lot of topics that you will see in other elective classes down the line. Violina is great, and the course discussion is always pointed and intelligent. Highly recommend!

The class session is too long and there is not enough content to adequately fill the session. The professor needs to integrate more videos, less lecture and more flexibility for arguments in cases. The guest speakers are so so. It would be nice if the materials were more recent and to have diversity in the cases.
Extremely easy course and professor

As context, this class is usually taught by a different professor who designed the course. Professor Armanini was asked to step in at the last minute, so the class has been a little disorganized as he got up to speed with the material. However, the professor is incredibly understanding and willing to work with the students to structure the class in a way so that we don't feel overwhelmed by courseload. There is a fair amount of reading for each class, but the cases and articles are generally pretty interesting.

There is a lot of interesing case work and discussions in this class. We have insightful conversations surrounding the business model canvas and value proposition canvas. We have also discussed emerging opportunities for new markets and company positioning. To note, it is very case and in-class participation heavy, so if that's not your thing, might not be your best bet.

This is what I imagined business school to be like...and is the first class I have taken where I can honestly say that is the case. The professor is lovely to start with and cares more about his students than grades, quizzes, etc. Class is entirely case/discussion based but is low pressure and Scott keeps the class (or those who want to be) engaged throughout. He focuses on learning rather than grading.

As many have said, this class is extremely easy and is nice to balance out heavier workload courses. However, I also find it boring and lacking in any structure. Scott stepped in as our professor when Dr. Rindova was appointed to Marshall's DEI committee, and while he is very nice and caring (he has adjusted assignments to reduce our workload), he's also been very unprepared and usually starts class late. We also just talk about the same innovative companies over and over - Uber, AirBnB, Amazon, DoorDash, Tesla, etc, and it's fairly suface level. The professor could do a better job at pushing people to think more critically or dive deeper. I feel you could learn a similar amount if you keep up to date with current business news.

The course is pretty low effort. There is a group project that goes for the whole semester and he basically takes you through the IDEO thing for innovating in a space you care about. You will do user interviews, research, prototyping, etc. There are cases but they're not overly mandatory to read. He coteaches with a Mckinsey consultant.

Not a ton of reading and super interesting cases (such as Uber, Braintrust, Etsy, etc). If you're at all interested in design thinking, you should definitely take this course as it realy is a ste-by-step guide on the process. Jim and Tiffany are incredibly smart and so open to chatting about any business ideas or problems you're trying to solve through a design thinking lens
I still have no idea what we're doing in this class.

The professors are a bit laissez-faire and the class isn't highly structured, so you have to put in the effort to engage with them, the readings, guest lectures (which are very interesting imo), etc. to get the most out of the course, but they are both accomplished and very knowledgeable about innovation and design thinking. You can learn a lot from them, especially if design thinking is new to you.

I agree with a lot of the other comments. If you love design thinking and want to interact a lot with the professors, go for it. Otherwise, this class is pretty much a waste of time. Readings are only lightly discussed, and the professor usually just says "So this is all pretty straightforward" instead of teaching you anything. It's also group heavy with substantial class time devoted to group work, so don't expect to spend a lot of time learning directly from the professor.

Its a pretty chilled class. You will spend most of the time working on your group project. Take this class if your interested in design thinking or if you want a low effort course to go with assignment heavy courses.

A pretty relaxed class overall. I think the design thinking portion is interesting but if you aren't open to that type of thinking then it may be burdensome. They have brought in some interesting guest speakers and I think the professors add good insights from their professional experiences. The group project is a huge part of the class so if that team is solid then your in a good spot!

The class teaches designed thinking. However the course is not really what I expected. The two instructors are great and respectful practitioners in the industry, but the way the class is structured did not really get the key concerpts across. I am quite confused by what we are supposed to do for our project.

This class has phenonmenal guest speakers and overall is a good exercise for finding product/market fit and pitching a new product idea. However it's stretched out over the entire semester and just feels like more work than what is really needed. Jim is a likeable guy and Tiffany is pretty remarkable, but sometimes it feels like they are over complicating the material for the sake of the class. You get to pick your own teams and if you choose a good product topic then at least it'll be semi interesting!

This class has a semester long project which is extremely helpful in thinking about how to create a product or service from just an idea. This professor is super nice, helpful, and really cares about students and their projects.

This class is basically a semester-long group project. If you like group work and coming up with new product/service ideas, you'll love it. If you're an independent worker, not interested in entrepreneurship, and/or looking to learn a lot of new, technical ideas to get the most out of your tuition dollars, look elsewhere. Legeman is good.

Useful to learn about design thinking, user interviews, market research, and doing the work of ideating/innovative thinking, but can feel like a slog amongst all the other classes with group projects. Legeman is fine but not great -- Vogel is great but not in person, at least not in this iteration. Other feedback from the 2024 folks is spot on.

Semester long group project, it is fun and you get to create a new product -- not exactly a ton of new material but Jim is a great professor. Make sure you choose an industry you are excited about, but its totally your choice.

This is a newly offered course. I think it's great! The class is primarily discussion-based and includes both individual and group projects/presentations. You are expected to participate in most (if not all) class discussions but it's commonly opinion-based.  The professor is open to everyone's viewpoints but usually doesn't tell you if you're right or wrong. There are no required readings. It's interesting to learn about established companies (not just startups) and evaluate how/why they pursue innovation. One drawback is the class can move very slowly at times, almost as if to fill the 3 hour time frame.

Ex-Deloitte Consultant teaches this class. He knows his stuff well and applies his past experiences to the class. Gives a sneak peek of how consulting is and how people in the industry think. Pretty light workload, just group presentations.

This class is valuable for strategic decision making, and understanding the logic (incentives) that come into play as a business leader attempting to structure deals and alliances with other businesses.

"Class would be good in theory; goes over corporate partnerships, as opposed to M&A. The class, however, is organized poorly. Professor spends way too long on case discussions, focusing too much on case-specific details. Lecture slides are saved for the last 5 - 10 minutes of class...extremely frustrating! 

The course goes over the same few points over and over; essentially keep each others' interests in mind and don't let people stab you in the back. A very easy class, but not as much learning as I would've hoped for."

"Kyle Mayer knows his stuff, and he does great work in putting this class together. Each lecture is interesting, and the way he structures the class and assignments is fair.

He's great, take this class. Readings are interesting on the whole and he keeps the lecture lively."

So so class. Easy workload. Great 2nd semester 2nd year class. Cases are cool, so if you dedicate yourself to the class the potential for growth is high. But like any strategy class, the material is really subjective, so be ready for that.

"I would take anything with Mayer. In a full term class, he is must less intense than he is in core.

Class is based on reading and participation. Very engaged classmates, fun environment, and intellectually stimulating."
Fairly interesting class as long as you do the reading. It's almost all participation so the workload is pretty low. Mayer talks really fast but he's a nice guy and the cases are pretty interesting.

Mayer is an engaging lecturer but most of the cases are tech related and it gets redundant. Student teams write cases and lead a discussion about it for ~1 hr. Its definitely one of the better classes here.
Fantastic class and professor. Learnt a lot in this class! Only con is that there are cases and readings for almost every class (not something you want in Sem 4).
I'm a huge Mayer fan, so I loved it. Great discussion and really cool cases about an essential topic.

Read cases and papers that focus on JVs, alliances, contracts, M&A. Mayer is a good professor - able to generate good classroom discussion. Final project is writing and teaching a case to the class. I believe that I will take a lot of what I learned from this class with me beyond business school.

Great professor, learn a lot. No cold calling, but a large % of your grade is based on participation. No midterm, no final, but you get to write a (group) case and present it, and that's 40% of the grade. Great cases, great discussions.
The class is a deeper dive into what strategy talks about. He brings in cool speakers and the cases are pretty interesting. I would take it again!
Kyle is great. Syllabus makes sense. It is hard to fully understand what I have walked away learning though.

Mayer's class is truly an MBA level class. He teaches strategy very well and really gets students to think out of the box. LOTS of cases to read, but interesting class discussions and not too much work. It's a great option for someone looking for a strategy class similar to Peer Fiss' core class.
Good not great. Mayer gets super excited and crams in a bunch during lectures but never really drives home the point. It is helpful to understand alliances though.
Kyle Mayer teaches this class. Take it!! Totally different from Global Strategy, and brilliant case studies..

This class is almost exactly like all the other strategy classes. Every class you read a case, and discuss. So readings for every class. You have to write a few papers throughout about cases, and do a presentation.  Work wise, it's mainly just readings.  Learning wise, after you discuss one case, the conversations all kind of become the same and you hear repeat information after the first few classes. Professor Mayer is a nice guy and energetic though, so he keeps it interesting.  If you need a moderate workload strategy class this one is good.
Excellent professor and great course for those who will manage relationships between companies.

This class was far outside my comfort zone, but I really enjoy Prof Mayer's energy.  The cases are interesting but there is a good amount of reading.  A lot depends on your classmates and how much they participate.  I really enjoy the group we have, and it's a great chance to practice making an argument in front of your peers.  Mayer will not let you off the hook and it's fun to be able to think on your feet.  Highly focused on entertainment.
When to partner with another firm, what that might look like, advantages and disadvantages.  Case heavy with interesting discussion opportunities.
Entertaining and fun class, especially as it is offered with only FT MBAs.

It's an interesting course but not sure how much I'm really learning. The cases are interesting and the course load is not bad at all. The course is structured mostly as open discussion about the case reading for the class session with a little bit of lecture to tie together patterns and basic learnings.

I used the lessons I learned in this class in multiple interviews. I love Mayer, the work load is a bit heavy (2 cases per week) but the class period is all discussion. We don't have "tests" but have a major group project where you get to write your own case. It's an awesome class taught by an incredible professor. If you don't take this class, take something else taught by Mayer before you graduate.

Kyle is awesome. The value of this class has a lot of correlation with quality of students who take the class.

If HiTech is your thing, this is a MUST-TAKE class.

Good: 
 You get to write a case for the class. Gives you a great insight into what goes into making all the cases that you read for classes.
 
 We all need to know about alliances and partnerships, considering a lot of us will be in senior management positions that require such knowledge, and some of the cases in this class do a great job of illustrating what works and what doesn't.
 
 Bad:
 Not a lot of students read the cases and Prof. Mayer lets everyone jump into the discussion so sometimes we just go off on tangents.
 
 Summary: Not a bad class but not a great class either. If you don't have any other option, go ahead and take it.

All you do is a read a case (every week) and argue about the alliances in the case. The class feels incredibly repetitive after about a month. I would stay clear - its very similar to the GSBA class that mayer taught during core
The course is repetitive and got boring after a while. I picked this course more for the time than for the interest. I wish I could say I took a lot from this class but I don't think I have.
Cases can be interesting, but also repetitive. Felt like a core class at time in terms of value of classmate discussion not always resonating.

Professor Mayer provides great cases and examples of very current alliances and corporate partnerships. It gets a little repetitive since it is all case-based, but it is a great opportunity to create and write your own case based on recent partnerships.
if you like professor Mayer and his teaching style you will enjoy this class.

The content is very relevant, as companies are forming new partnerships, alliances, or mergers / acquisitions every day. Unlike some of the other courses, this class takes a conceptual point of view to alliances or mergers.
Workload is pretty light. A lot of in class discussion and readings.
Great class. Not too much work.

Mayer is always great, especially after core. This class is somewhat of a repeat of his core class. Not really the topics necessarily but the way he teaches and the format of the class. Cool thing is you get to write and present a case in this class, so it the most unique project you will get in any MBA class.

Kyle is a great professor! He always brings alot of enthusiasm to his classes and each of this lectures are structured perfectly. I highly recommend this class to anyone (1st and 2nd years) since the information you are taught is relevant to all areas of business and industries.
There are alot of case readings but next to no HW and a group project and a final paper.
This has been one of my favorite classes at Marshall. The professor is great and the case readings are very interesting and insightful.

I found the takeaways from the first month to be useful/interesting but the same structure of the class each week (case discussion) gets mundane/predictable after a while. Part of the class is writing a case and teaching note then leading the class discussion for the case, which is a nice change of pace from typical presentations we're used to and not as much work as it sounds like it might be.

This has been one of my favorite classes at Marshall. Professor Mayer is extremely engaging and does a great job of integrating more current cases into the curriculum. Classes are all discussion driven which I prefer to a traditional lecture format and the final project is the most unique one I've been assigned during my time at Marshall. Highly recommend for all regardless of your target career function.
Mayer is good at facilitating case discussions but the same format over and over gets really old really fast. Assignments aren't too tough and cases are interesting for the most part. Good takeaways.
Honestly it's a chill, interesting, class. You get out of it what you put into it. This is never the reason I'm stressed out about school. Great class to balance out a heavy quant schedule

Course Content: Do not evaluate based on concepts learned. If that was the only criterion, this would be worth 1.5 units. But there is a lot more that happens in terms of case discussions and a variety of perspectives. That's where the learning is, as it should be for a MBA program. Professor: Very enthusiastic about the subject. Has the confidence and knowledge to back that enthusiasm. Interesting assignments. Really encourages you to think. Warning: This will not be a class for which you think "I can sail through this doing nothing". There are some who do it but very difficult. Expect lots of case readings.

Kyle mayer is one of the best professors at Marshall. It is a discussion based class and you need to do the reading for every class, but the cases are very enjoyable. The workload is very managable and everyone should take this class at some point
Yes, alliance is a huge portion of company strategy.  Even if I do not directly deal with alliance, I can apply the concepts and examples I learned from this class to serve my clients.
Yes, the ability to look at great use-cases surrounding alliances, partnerships, and acquisitons around the world will help any would-be business professional.

I took this class mostly because I really enjoyed Mayer in core, and he excels at facilitating discussion. I loved that this was one of few classes that touched on private sector interaction with the public sector and nonprofits. I have enjoyed getting the practice of writing a case with my team (a major part of the course). The guest speakers have mostly been really interesting with practical experience. Overall, there are a few core lessons that are echoed again and again with cases, which I guess is kind of the point. I think it's a nice class for learning how to think about things.

No midterm or final. Just 2 papers, a final paper, and a group project. Case reading before most classes, but you not reading them doesn't hurt much just makes it harder to participate in class. Takes attendance and participation is worth ~20-25%. Overall course learnings are great, applicable to all facets of business. Recommend this class, even if you want to put 50% effort into the readings/participation.

Kyle is an awesome, gregarious professor. The class is almost entirely discussion based. Kyle facilitates robust discussions of the case each class. I was a bit disappointed because I wanted to get more tangible knowledge from Kyle but he never lectures and you're just getting opinions on alliances from your fellow classmates. Not a hard no just not what I wanted out of the experience.

Discussion based class, very few deliverables. Professor is both relaxed and extremely knowledgeable. Also has some interesting guest speakers. Agree with the comment that it might also be too discussion based and not enough lecture from the professor. Still highly recommend.
discussion based class; professor is friendly and supportive. the guest speakers area also good, and the professor has a deep network

Heavy class discussion is a double-edged sword. Sometimes you learn, and sometimes you're just listening to people talk. If you liked Peer Fiss or Shon Hiatt, you're likely to be disappointed here. If you hated those guys, this could be perfect as a lower stakes way to explore strategy.

Personally, I find a little more tangible knowledge from a professor to be helpful. The style is in contrast to the core strat course that Peer fiss has. Too much discussion and no concrete framework/analysis does little justice. But the course is very accomodating and kudos to prof kyle for allowing zoom participation.

I really like the structure of the class and the discussion-focus. Professor does send summary emails after every class to clarify key takeaways from the cases. No exams. 1 group project and 3 short individual assignments.

This class was super interesting from the cases we read to the discussions that followed. There is not a ton of work which is nice but you do have to prepare a full case with a group of students (not as hard as you would expect). The guest speakers are also great.

The class is vey discussion and case focused, which made it a very practical application to theory. The guest speakers brought in interesting perspectives from fascinating industries, which helped further understand theoretical strategy within an organization.

This class is purely case discussion based so if you don't read the cases it will be hard to particpate/engage in class. However, it's a fun class environment and the professor is really engaging. There's one big group project where you have to write a case and then lead a class discussion which is cool.
Great class covering mostly interesting alliances/partnerships. Professor Mayer does a good job of stimulating discussion.

Pros: there are just a couple of short individual assignments and one group assignment; case-based class but the professor doesn't cold call, so you don't have to do a lot of work if you don't want to. Con: Because this isn't a super demanding class and the professor doesn't cold call, some lectures can be a bit boring with most of the class unengaged.

Mayer is a good discussion leader and brings the energy. The problem is the class doesn't have enough content/insights to justify itself. There are a few key takeaways from the course that keep getting reinforced over and over. There are diminishing returns after the first few weeks of class. This should be a 1.5 unit course, not a full 3.0.
Not much work and largely case based discussion. I would agree that there aren't enough key takeaways or insights.

Not too many learnings, but Mayer is fantastic and the cases generally interesting. Agreed it should be a 1/2 semester course as the objectives and learnings are generally achieved early and repeated often the rest of the course. Super light on work.

The professor is really great. This is a class that is all that you make of it. If you read the cases and are actively partcipating then you do get a lot out of it. He is a great guy and wants everyone to learn. Depends mainly on class discussion.
Easy Class and kind of informative - good to take for light class

This class is easy; no midterm, two papers and one final paper (total of 3), and one group case presentation. This professor is full of himself and loves to hear himself talk - you are not learning any new material in class, it is just the same basic framework repeated every time. BUT if you want a low lift course this is for you

Class can be as engaging or unegaging as you make it -- entirely case based and the work is participating. 3 assignments (2 short written papers and 1 group case that you then present on). Kyle has good insights.

Kyle is a great professor. He works hard to make the class engaging and the material is overall interesting asides from a few less interesting cases. The case-based method can be a daunting class approach and can be a slow way of learning, but he does his best to make it accessible, especially as students are eventually intended to lead a case as their main group assignment. Be prepared for a Friday session of courses sometime during the semester that will replace a few normal classes to accomodate speakers.

The amount of assignment to turn in is light and approachable. No grades have been released yet so nothing can be said on the toughness of grading.
Who is this class for? Any student looking to understand how organizations can work together to achieve goals. Applicable to all industries.
Final Thoughts: Professor Mayer is an excellent moderator of discussions and is extremely knowledgeable. The class is worth it alone to learn from him.

career: Consulting; Technology; Entrepreneurship | ITech-driven entrepreneurship and technology consulting
comments:
Overall, course is case-based and not too many graded assignments throughout the course of the semester, so unsure about how grading is. 
Who is this class for? Those interested in partnerships and/or company synergies.
Final Thoughts: Some cases are more interesting than others, but if you are someone who dislikes reading cases before each class and then talking about them, this might not be for you.

career: Consulting; Marketing | Consulting > Customer & Product Marketing
comments:
You have to lead a case discussion with your group which makes up most of your grade.
Who is this class for? If you enjoy case discussions, pre-reading or atleast skimming the cases and participating/actively listening. It teaches you a lot about diverse industries and their alliance design!
Final Thoughts:

Easy, just readings and class discussions with minimal amount of group work. Hybrid, so many people tuned in via zoom.
Who is this class for? People interested in M&A and strategy
Final Thoughts: I enjoyed this class, but is easy to tune out and skate by. Definitely not challenging.

career: Consulting | Additionally Supply Chain and Operations
comments:
This course thus far is completely case based and thus has a lot of reading. So some areas are hard to gauge/ subjective 
Who is this class for? Most useful for consulting and finance 
Final Thoughts: This has been my favorite course in this MBA program. Its all reading, discussion and critical thinking. The professor poses many questions and forces us to think strategically

The class was good at attending to our schedules and wasn't too intensive. 
Who is this class for? A student who wants to be involved in business strategy should take this course. 
Final Thoughts: Professor Mayer is great and I will always highly recommend him to any student.

Kyle is an amazing professor! The cases are dense though so definitely be prepared reading them as discussion is a huge part of this course 
Who is this class for? A truly interested student, don't take it if you don't come to class because he's amazing
Final Thoughts: Kyle is an amazing professor, I honestly can say I have learned so so much

This class is very interactive and closely connected to our everyday lives. You often see brands collaborate and launch new products or services that either raise a lot of questions or create strong appeal that didn’t exist before. This course helps you think more strategically about mergers and acquisitions around you, whether in the past, present, or future. The professor leads the class in a way that’s easy to follow, so anyone can participate and share their thoughts. Even just listening to the discussions, you leave with new insights and real-world examples of mergers and acquisitions you may not have considered before.

Kyle Mayer makes the course engaging and is helpful in outlining tangible takeaways from cases. Coursework includes reading the cases before discussions, studying for midterm and final, and writing a case as a group project.
Take this class with Kyle Mayer if possible. Useful regardless of career choice. Good way to think about business relationships at the corporate level.

This is a hybrid course so you have the option to Zoom into the class. Usually half of the class ends up Zooming in which makes it a bit awkward for them to participate. Every class is a different case. The group assignment is to create a case on an alliance/acquisition and lead a class discussion. These can be hit or miss. Kyle Mayer is a really great guy and very knowledgeable in the content. Personally, I wish he lectured more and offered some sort of framework to ground the case discussions.

Kyle's class is very interactive and requires student participation. The cases are across pop media, telecommunications, travel etc so there is something for everyone. You get a chance to be a teacher for the class and lead a case discussion yourself - this was my favourite part.
Professor is engaging. Course gets very repetitive after a few case studies.
Great course.

The professor is great and the class very super interactive. But unfortunately there very few takeaways / learnings from this course. You will enjoy the course, but on restrospection you would not be able to state any major learnings given the number of cases we go through.

career: Consulting, Strategy roles in multi industry
comments: It's very effective. Read the material every day and participate. You will do great. It's such a good course and Kyle puts a lot of thought into it. It is not too hard too just smart work, not hard work. The paper and doing it with a team is one of my favorite things I have done this semester or year as a class project.

This is one of the most challenging classes I have taken, and it is also one of the best classes. This strategy course has taught me to approach decisions is a more thoughtful, strategic way. I think this course will significantly influence my decision-making process in my future job. This class is a lot of work, so only sign up for it if you are passionate about the material.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: Must attend classes, a lot of reading and work on a weekly basis, but the strategic and critical thinking skills built through the process are well worth it!
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: Sweet class. Teacher is extremely smart, no-BS, straight to the point. Forces you to look at the challenges of sustainability through the eyes of management (looking at the other challenges such as profit, stakeholders, implementation etc.). One of the most useful classes I've taken at Marshall. More practical than theory. One of the best teachers. You'll learn a lot, regardless of your view on sustainability.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: Class was a waste of time. Its just another strategy class through the lens of environmental sustainability. I was very excited to take this class and was very disappointed. A lot of work with not a lot of reward. Adler doesn't really teach. Students present their team interpretation of the case. 2 student presentations per class and Adler provides commentary. He drills down into his single framework for the whole semester. One plus is he is very responsive to feedback. During mid-year review, the entire class complained about the work and he cut it down substantially. Also, no tests or quizzes, just lots of little assignments due every week and a big project at the end of the semester.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: The amount of work in this class is beyond unacceptable. There's a case + essay on the case + 2-4 readings + essays on each reading + posted take aways after class EVERY WEEK. The content is interesting, but you have 1-2 teams presenting on the case each class (meaning you have to present on 2 cases throughout the semester - not joking on the amount of work) and there are a lot of non-FT MBA students in the class which is obnoxious. You have to really love the content to make it even sort of worth while, which I do, but even then, this class is miserable.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: There is LOTS of readings, and the professor requires you to write a case note & reading note before class, and take-away note after class... If you are interested into environmental sustainability and company "green commitment" and PR strategy in environment topics, you should take this. If you want to leave more time for recruitment, don't take the class, it takes tooo much time. If you just want to board your insight and learn something different, take it! you will learn a lot!
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: This professor is excellent, one of the best at Marshall. Probably the best strategy course I've taken at Marshall, the cases are interesting and the professor really challenges students to learn and get better. This course is hard, not necessarily in its grading but in the amount of assignments and reading, so be prepared for that. If you are interested in sustainability at all this is a must take course
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: this professor is the worst i've ever experienced at Marshall. no offense to the person above, but the professor is terrible. he has no background in sustainability and is not addative whatsoever in class. there is an absurd amount of work and the professor doesn't actually teach. avoid Adler at all cost.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: The most time-consuming course I have taken at Marshall, but it is a great course for people interested to know more about the different aspects of sustainability today. The syllabus covers all relevant aspects of sustainability, and there is focus on ESG, GRI, LEED etc. The course focuses more on knowledge transfer than on the strategy aspect of it, hence it might be more useful to understand the industry as a whole. If you have heavy coursework in other courses, beware as this course has too much workload.
topic_title: MOR 566 - Environmental Sustainability and Competitive Advantage

comments: This course is kinda overscored by many students. I didn't learn much that I hadn't known before. There are a lot of annoying readings. If you've never taken a soft skills class, go for it.

Love this class. Basically teaching you how people function and how to use it to your advantage. The only thing I don't love is some of the exercises seem meaningless. The professor is engaging and the readings are well curated.

The content is really interesting, and Professor Fast clearly has a passion and knows how to present in a compelling way. However, I found some of the role play and simulations a little juvenile and just frankly annoying in a 6:30-9:30pm class. However, the guest speakers are great and the readings are really valuable.

My favorite class I've taken at Marshall. Fast is clearly one of the best professors we have. His class is exactly the type of class I came to business school for. Interesting cases, assignments, and speakers. He also is personable and has great answers to difficult questions. I also appreciate that he takes being a professor very seriously, and obviously loves what he does.

Tools discussed can be applied immediately during your MBA and taken with you once you graduate. I think this course (like others have noted) is a must-take. But only with Professor Fast. If you're on the fence, download the book "Power: Why Some People Have It And Others Don't" This book will give a sense of the topics and lessons discussed.
helpful course but the class spends lots of time discussing people's opinions and experiences. the book is interesting and could be a decent substitute for the course imo
Be ready for some introspection! Great mix of cases, covering individuals with different approaches to power.

The course provides some helpful techniques and a framework for thinking of influence/power but feels very "white male centric" - not sure how much of these techniques are applicable to women. It also feels really redundant. Seems like it should be a 1.5 credit class

The case studies and material are interesting reads. I did not come into the class expecting a lot of lectures because this is not a topic that can be taught in the traditional sense. It is a soft skill that we are trying to develop and the breakout rooms and refelction exercises serve the purpose they are meant to serve.

The entirety of this course could be summarized in just a speaker session. It just repeats over and over with the same case with different people. In the past, this class was apparently focused on bringing in interesting speakers, however in the online setting this has shifted to cases and not for the better. Definitely should be a 1.5 credit, it's a huge waste of time as a 3 credit class.

If you actually take the time to dive deep on the exercises, class discussions, and readings this can one of the most valuable MBA classes. However, you need to invest the time. If you just show up to class it really becomes very repetitive.
I wish the cases were more diversified and the lectures were a bit more structured. We are half way trough and I feel that either the cases became repetitive, or the discussion became superficial. Regardless, I still recommend the class.

This class is a complete and utter waste of time and money. I've never been so disappointed in a class in my life. If you just want to sit in a breakout room for 3 hours until 930pm to chit chat with your classmates then take this class. The professor barely does any actual teaching (maybe every 2-3 weeks he'll teach a topic or theory for 5 minutes) and just puts us in breakout rooms to do stupid and pointless exercises that he never connects back to any learnings. There's a lot of reading but he never brings up or reinforces anything from the readings. Also the book that everyone says is great (Power: Why Some People Have It and Others Don't) is super archaic and reinforces frustrating gender stereotypes. As an example, the author of the book said Anita Hill continued to spend time with Clarence Thomas because she wanted to personally gain/benefit from being around him. A complete victim-blame. It's upsetting that this book is actually being used to teach business leaders in 2020.

An excellent course and professor. The real value of the class is not in lecture but in the activities that force you to debate and consider your actions and how they can help you as a person and in your career. The readings are interesting, even if they are not as discussed in class too much; think of them as a course supplement. Difficulty is not too high, but the value is largely what you put into the class - some opt to sit on the sidelines or turn off their cameras, but doing so is a missed opportunity to be engaged and grow. I feel the most engaged in this class of all my classes. There is value in this course for anyone who wishes to grow in character and confidence. The watchword for this class is empowerment, not victimhood - this is a nice change of pace from cultural fads that emphasize blaming others for lack of success.

A good course that isn't too heavy. The assignments are not too heavy, and the interviews for people in power are pretty valuable. Would like to have had more solid takeaways and directly applicable methods/techniques though.

You'll develop of framework for maneuriving life/relationships that will increase the likelihood that you'll accumulate more power. You can probably get this yourself from reading the Pfeffeer Power book though. The class will help reinforce it and increase your chances at implementing the suggestions in your life.
Only off thing about this course is the role-playing, not sure how it connects to the class, but its not a deal-breaker.
This class is very east but painful to get through. The questions for group discussion are not well thought through and are quite low in terms of need for critical thinking. Very skippable

This is one of those courses that you're going to get out of it what you put into it; if you actually do the readings (less the cases) and try to practice the tactics, you have the opportunity to really develop the skills that will serve you in your career. Prof. Bresnahan is a lot more flexible than Prof Fast, so is really on you to make the most of it as his teaching style can make it feel like it's not worth it to put in much effort.

This class doesn't do a great job at thinking through the nuances of power. While this class has some helpful lessons, and forces you to do some good self-reflection, this class could do a much better job of thinking through power in a more intersectional lens. That being said, it's probably one of the easier classes at Marshall - not a ton of readings and the write-ups are incredibly easy

Concepts and frameworks are useful, but there is not enough discussion around how they may (or may not) work for anyone who isn't a cis white man. There is some diversity represented in the cases, but not enough in my opinion. At its foundation the class is pretty good, but there is a lot of room for improvement. Professor cold calls .
Interesting material, but there are a lot of assignments.  He also cold calls so you should probably keep up with the reading.

Overall concepts are useful. Professor Fast cold calls every single class in an attempt to exert power, even if other students are raising their hand to contirbute.  He also doesn't tend to appreciate diverse opinions and will stick to his own thoughts when questioned.

Fast created the course and is passionate about the material. He is a bit old school (despite being young) in terms of how he runs lectures (no cell phones, cold calling, etc.), but brings unique perspectives and good material to every class. Interesting cases.

This class is sorta just for fun. It's easy, the workload is light and professor is nice, but I wouldn't say there's a whole lot of value to be gained. Much of the value can come from hanging out in class and talking to different people and networking

I think most people take Chris's classes as a fluff class to offset other classes' workloads. He's really nice, but I agree with the above comment that you're better off choosing another class if you want your true tuition's worth of money.

I disagreed with the book on a few occasions and the topics attempt to paint with broad strokes about very intricate situations that deal with power. I don't believe this class gets things wrong, but it is a little tough to get exposure to unique situations (like political situations that will be common in corporate life) when considering this class. Maybe a bit less helpful than originally thought, but these are good topics to consider

Easy course just like other courses of Chris. There is not whole lot of learning in this course. Most of the content overlaps with his other courses. Take it if you want to offset your heavy assignment courses.

Chris is a really nice guy, but the substance in this class is seriously lacking. I was hoping it would be similarly good to Wiltermuth's Negotiations class, and it's worse on every level. The book for this class is a joke, lecture has little content or clear application, and practicing "using power" is mostly contained to an ill-defined project. Class is easy though.
Professor Heino also offer this class in Fall - great class with a lot of discussion and interation. Reading can be a bit long.

It's a fluffy class.  Useful general concepts but everything seems pretty intuitive and the assignments don't advance my learning.  Interesting topics but more of a basic conversation than a grad-level learnign environment.  Also Becky is rad.

A lot of assigned readings, most of which we don't ever discuss during class. Workload is manageable once you realize you don't need to complete 90% of the assigned readings. Some interesting takeaways but I wouldn't classify this class as a "must take".
Chris is exceptional - super knowledgeable with incredible anecdotes from his career.
Easy class Chris is great! He is easy going and the class is so easy like u don't even need to go lol
Openly expresses his political views in class.

You do learn a couple interesting things but to be honest the professor is a bit dull and does a lot to portray this image of being a family man to us. I've heard this class is incredible with Nate Fast but I unfortunately didn't have the opportunity to take it with him

Professor Bresnehan is fantastic, but this class is fairly relaxed. There are a few tips and tricks that are helpful to keep in mind from this class, but overall it is a long form discussion about how people develop and exercise power

It depends on what you want to get out of the class. If you want a chill class where half the people go to and minimal work then it is for you. I wished I would get more lecture and actual useful information and strategies but I find in class that we are just chatting with our peers more than learning from the lecutre.
Great Class and professor. Easy class and informative

Great professor who teaches great life skills. Yes this is an easier "senioritis" class, but the professor is really cool and tries really hard to teach relevant concepts. I really enjoyed this class and learned a lot. Favorite class this semester.

This course is not very challenging at all. Chris is probably the chillest professor on campus. Because the class is very discussion heavy, we do hear a lot of different perspectives that encourage us to approach situations differently. If you want a chill class, absolutely take this with Chris.

Chris is a great teacher. Not a heavy workload, and he keeps you engaged for the whole 3-hour class. Definitely alot of participation needed but its broken into smaller groups and class discussion which is nice.
Who is this class for? This class is a fun and easy elective to take and looking at psychology perspective in business world of topics about power.
practical advice about building networks, communication strategies etc. not much courseload.

Easy class, fun with Professor Bresnahan. Good way to think about power and influence. More of a self help class than a business class, but useful both in the skills it provides in my opinion, as well as easing your workload for the semester.
I'm impressed how useful this class has been. Prof. Voss was a FBI hostage negotiator and he does a great job applying hostage negotiating to business.

All of the content we learned in this course was taught in the first class. Professor Voss spends most of our class time repeating the same concepts and telling anecdotes, trying to fill time. We also spend a lot of the class role playing, which gets very old. This class hasn't been useful enough to be a 3 credit full semester course.
Sometimes classes take 45 min to even get started. Lots of just sitting around.

"So this is a great, great course and can be attributed to a lot of my success in recent business type transactions and acts as a wicked Jedi mind trick in winning 'nothing fights' with the girlfriend. It's also helped personal relationships significantly through thinking more empathetically. And the professor is great. Former suicide hotline operator turned FBI hostage negotiator with a sense of humor. I have zero doubt this guy knows what he's talking about. 

However, it's too long. This should be a 1.5 credit course or, at the very least, not three hours at a time. We harp on the same topic for a long time. Maybe this is necessary as they're important topics, but sometimes boredom eclipses wonder. 

Still, take this course. It is fantastically necessary for success. Of that I have no doubt."
Class is terrible. You don't learn anything. Terrible waste of tuition dollars.
really useful class both for negotiations and leadership in general. Not heavy workload, just regular assignments due each week.
Good soft skills class to take. Prof knows his stuff and teaches well. Each class has a practice negotiation so you get real practice in negotiations.
Great course. Gets a little repetitive and could thus be restructured to a half course, but definitely a useful course to take with a great lecturer.
Good class - First few weeks were the best. Started to wane towards the back end but professor does bring a unique twist with his FBI background

Sprinkled into his lectures may be some actual good advice completely founded on anecdotes with some politically incorrect language posing as knowledge and research. I don't care that he was a "top negotiator for the FBI", being a good athlete doesn't make you a good coach. It feels like a 3 hour long infomercial to buy his book or hire his company. "Let me tell you about this time..." Try another teacher maybe?
Conceptually a great course, should be a 1.5 though, runs out of steam after the first three classes.

The discussions and negotiation excercises are a great chance for you to directly apply the techniques learned in the classroom and see their real impact. The prof is good and experienced in the real world and, although the class is highly repetitive in terms of what you read on the book, it has important takeaways. Things you'll need in different aspects of your life!

Everyone should take a negotiations class as the things taught work for any career. This class provides some interesting tricks and tips to negotiate with other people.  Voss is an interesting character. Sometimes the information in class tends to repeat itself, but a lot of getting comfortable with negotiations is just practicing a lot.

Professor has mastered a distinct skill and can convey his techniques effectively.  This course feels like it could be a 1.5 hour course.  "Tools" provided from this class feel like they will be useful for a long time.
The course should be a 1.5 unit course, because the class is redundant after week 5.

This class can get a little bit repetitive but I think the concepts can be applied and his stories are interesting. The course load is not heavy or difficult - you just practice a case negotiation with a classmate every week and write about a couple negotiations you've done.
Yes. Although I find little value in the class discussions and projects, the mock interview practice is rewarding.

A majority of this course was actual negotiations; however, performance in these activities had no impact on grade.  

Negotiation is a skill that everyone will need in the real world and getting more practice is definitely recommended.

Regardless of career path, learning to negotiate is extremely important. This course offers a lot of role playing experience to learn how to negotiate. However, how the content is taught and student evaluation could be better.

Negotiation is an applied skill and is almost an art when it comes to application. A seasoned practitioner like Voss definitely has the best skills in this subject matter. However, it's quite different to teach in a classroom from in practicing. I don't think the effectiveness of learning is up to my expectation.
Voss said he will not be back :(

Voss is very different from other professors. He doesn't use Blackboard and won't chase you. He's a former FBI hostage negotiator. He gives basics of negotiations and tools, gives a lot of examples, talks about different scenarios. We practice every week in pairs negotiating some reals cases. Many students say that the material becomes repetitive after the first several lectures but I find it even useful. Negotiation skills are hard to develop if they are not natural, so I prefer some repetition.
The hardest part is to apply these skills in practice. The course helps a lot.
The only problem is that Chris doesn't give much feedback, which makes it more difficult to improve. It's better to ask for feedback. I took this class based on the recommendation of my friend from Georgetown and don't regret. It's been one of the best classes I've taken so far.
Good class. Not too much work. Some practical info and it's good practice to negotiate each week in an unfamiliar setting. The professor is great.
This should be a required course. The content is relevant for any industry and Kim is passionate about the subject matter.
Great soft skills course that is practically taught with a good balance of theory.
Great class. Everyone should know how to negotiate.

This class provides lots of practices you can hardly get anywhere else in Marshall. Not so much to be learn during the lectures though. It's a good start to work on your negotiation skills if you haven't take it as a real topic yet.

Coombs is nice, but not engaging. Probably should have already retired. The content of this class is still useful though, so it's still worth taking although you could probably learn just as much reading the book on your own (but who really does that?)

HIGHLY RECOMMEND. I learned more practical skills in this class than any other class in business school. It's highly interactive, but not stressful. Most prep is done during class time, and there is very little in the way of assignments - but that doesn't stop you from learning a lot! Tost is a GREAT professor. I wish I could take this class again.

This has by far been one of the best classes I've ever taken. We do a negotiation every class and the material builds on itself. Prof Tost brings SO much energy to this course and really engages students during the post-negotiation discussions. You don't want to miss this class!

This course is fantastic - very interactive and teaches important skills in a way that forces you to really understand how you think and teaches you to adapt your style in a way that will better serve your goals. Professor Tost is amazing and cares a lot about the course and students! She makes the important takeaways very clear and really adapts to feedback. Assignments are pretty simple: a negotiation journal (notes on the negotiations you conduct from the first half of the semester), one prep document for a negotiation, a team negotiation memo, and a final reflection.

The semester isn't even over and I've already learned so much from this class! Class is very interactive, with negotiation exercises each week + time for peer feedback. Professor is very engaging and clear about the key takeaways.

This is a fantastic class! Professor Tost is so engaging and incredibly knowledgeable. There is a negotiation with varying partners every week, some reading (fairly light though), and sometimes there are short videos to watch. The negotiations during class are definitely where you learn a huge amount because you're truly getting hands-on practice. After the negotiation, there is a debrief with the class and time for one-on-one feedback with your negotiating counterpart. You also get to see the results of the entire class and how you and your counterpart did compared to the class. Overall, would highly recommend this class, especially with Professor Tost!

I love this class! As someone who gets pretty uncomfortable in negotiations or confrontational situations, this class really shifted my mindset. You get to practice in a stress-free enviornment and learn from your classmates during the debrief on creative ways to bridge differences between you and the party you are negotiating with. Prof. Tost is also very understanding and tries her best to provide resources for us to succeed.
